Foundations

Everything between "I have never written a line of code" and "I can be trusted with a real Python codebase." The language itself, the data structures you will use every day, the standard library that means you rarely need a dependency, and the tools — a debugger, a test suite, a type checker, a linter — that separate code that runs from code that can be relied on.

How to use this course

  • This course assumes no prior programming experience. It starts at "how do I run a file" and finishes with a working command-line application that has tests and an exit status. If you already write Python comfortably, go to the Python Mastery course instead — it starts where this one stops.
  • Everything here targets Python 3.14 (released October 2025). Everything also works on 3.12 and later; where a feature is newer than 3.10 the version that introduced it is stated inline, because you will be reading code written for older interpreters for years to come.
  • Type the examples rather than copying them. Typing surfaces the small mistakes that copying hides, and every one of those is something you would otherwise meet later under worse conditions. Every output block in this course was produced by actually running the code above it.
  • Run something after every few lines. The commonest beginner mistake is writing thirty lines before running anything, then facing an error with thirty candidate causes.
  • Each section is Concept → Mechanism → Practice → Exercises with solutions. Do the exercises. They are where the material stops being something you have read and becomes something you can do.
  • Set yourself up before section 1:
python3 --version          # 3.12 or newer for the whole course
mkdir -p ~/python-foundations && cd ~/python-foundations
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate

Versions every output block in this course was produced against: Python 3.14.4, on Linux.

What you are actually learning

Not a list of syntax. Five ideas that explain almost everything a beginner finds confusing, and that keep paying off for as long as you write Python:

  1. Names are labels on objects. Assignment moves a label; mutation changes the object. A list that "changed by itself", a default argument that remembers its last call and a function that modifies its caller's data are one mechanism seen from three angles (§2, §4).
  2. Every container has a job and a cost. A list for order, a dictionary for lookup, a set for membership, a tuple for a fixed record — and x in some_list inside a loop is the most common slowdown in ordinary Python, because a list is searched item by item and a set is not (§6–§7, §15).
  3. Iteration can be lazy. The iterator protocol, generators and comprehensions let a program hold one item at a time instead of a million — and an iterator that has been used up stays used up (§8).
  4. Failure is designed, not discovered. Narrow except clauses, exceptions that name the offending value, and with blocks that make cleanup impossible to forget (§9–§10).
  5. Working code is proven, not hoped. A debugging procedure instead of staring, tests aimed at the boundaries, type hints a checker verifies, and a linter that runs without being asked (§14).

By the end you should be able to build, test and ship a small command-line program — the capstone in §16 is one — and read someone else's Python and explain why it behaves the way it does.

SECTION 1

Running Python

Before anything else, you need to be able to run code and see what it does. That sounds trivial and it is where a surprising number of people get stuck for a week — not because the ideas are hard, but because "which Python is this", "why can't it find my file" and "what does this error mean" are questions nobody answers up front. This section answers them. By the end of it you will have an interpreter, a project directory, an editor that helps rather than hinders, and the ability to read the three errors you will meet on your first day.

1.1 Two Ways to Run Code

Python gives you an interactive interpreter — the REPL, for read, evaluate, print, loop — and the ability to run a script from a file. You will use both, constantly, for different things.

The REPL starts when you run python3 with no arguments:

$ python3
Python 3.14.4 (main, Jun 18 2026, 14:25:02) [GCC 15.2.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> 2 + 2
4
>>> name = 'Ada'
>>> name.upper()
'ADA'
>>> len(name)
3
>>> _ + 1
4
>>> exit()
$

Four things to notice. The >>> is the prompt, and it is not part of what you type. An expression's value is printed automatically — name.upper() showed 'ADA' without a print, which is true only in the REPL. The value is shown with quotes, because the REPL prints the repr (§11.8) rather than the string itself. And _ is a REPL-only name holding the last result, which is handy for continuing a calculation.

Leave with exit(), quit(), or Ctrl-D on Linux and macOS (Ctrl-Z then Enter on Windows).

help() works on anything and is the fastest documentation you have:

>>> help(len)
Help on built-in function len in module builtins:

len(obj, /)
    Return the number of items in a container.

>>> dir(str)[-8:]
['rstrip', 'split', 'splitlines', 'startswith', 'strip', 'swapcase', 'title', 'translate']

Use the REPL to answer a question: does this method exist, what does this return, is this string really what I think. Use a script for anything you want to keep. A script is a plain text file with a .py extension:

$ cat hello.py
name = 'Ada'
print(f'Hello, {name}!')
print('This is a script.')

$ python3 hello.py
Hello, Ada!
This is a script.

The difference that catches everyone once: in a script, nothing is printed unless you print it.

$ cat quiet.py
2 + 2
'a string'
len('abc')

$ python3 quiet.py
$

Three expressions were evaluated and their values thrown away. In the REPL each would have shown a result. That auto-display is a REPL convenience, not a language feature.

1.2 Which Python Is Running?

This is the single most common source of early confusion, so settle it before writing anything.

$ python3 --version
Python 3.14.4

$ which python3
/usr/bin/python3

$ python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.executable); print(sys.version_info[:3])"
/usr/bin/python3
(3, 14, 4)

python3 -c 'code' runs a snippet without a file, and it is the fastest way to ask the interpreter about itself.

On most systems python3 is what you want and python may not exist at all, or may be an old Python 2. Machines commonly have several Pythons — one from the operating system, one from a package manager, one per project. When something behaves inexplicably, sys.executable tells you which one is actually running, and it is right more often than your memory of what you installed.

This course targets Python 3.14. Everything in it works on 3.12 and later; where a feature is newer than 3.10 the version is stated inline, because you will be reading code written for older interpreters for years.

python3 -m module runs a module as a program, and it is worth knowing on day one because a great deal of Python tooling is invoked that way:

$ echo '{"b":2,"a":1}' | python3 -m json.tool
{
    "b": 2,
    "a": 1
}

$ python3 -m venv .venv          # create a virtual environment
$ python3 -m pip install ruff    # install a package
$ python3 -m http.server 8000    # serve the current directory
$ python3 -m timeit '"".join(["a"] * 100)'

The advantage over the bare command is that -m guarantees you are using the module belonging to the interpreter you just named, which matters as soon as more than one Python exists (§12.9).

1.3 Files, Directories and the Path

python3 hello.py looks for hello.py relative to the directory you are in, not relative to where the file lives or where Python is installed.

$ pwd
/home/ada

$ python3 hello.py
python3: can't open file '/home/ada/hello.py': [Errno 2] No such file or directory

$ ls
projects

$ cd projects/first-steps
$ ls
hello.py

$ python3 hello.py
Hello, Ada!

That error message is unusually good: it prints the full path it tried, so the fix is almost always visible in the message itself. When it says /home/ada/hello.py and your file is in /home/ada/projects/first-steps/, you are in the wrong directory.

A path with no leading / is relative to the current directory; one starting with / (or C:\ on Windows) is absolute. Both work:

$ python3 projects/first-steps/hello.py
Hello, Ada!

$ python3 /home/ada/projects/first-steps/hello.py
Hello, Ada!

Set yourself up with a directory to work in:

mkdir -p ~/python-foundations
cd ~/python-foundations

Everything in this course can live there. §12.10 covers how a real project is laid out; for now one directory is enough.

1.4 A Script That Runs Itself

On Linux and macOS a script can be made directly executable with a shebang — a first line naming the interpreter — plus the executable permission:

$ cat greet.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
print('Hello from an executable script')

$ chmod +x greet.py
$ ./greet.py
Hello from an executable script

Write #!/usr/bin/env python3, not #!/usr/bin/python3. The env form searches your PATH, so it finds the Python in an activated virtual environment (§12.8); the hard-coded path always uses the system one, which is usually the wrong answer and always the less portable one.

The shebang must be the very first line — before any comment, blank line or docstring — or it is just a comment. It has no effect on Windows and no effect when the file is run as python3 greet.py, so including it costs nothing.

1.5 Source Encoding

A .py file is UTF-8 by default, which means you can put any character you like in a string or a comment without saying anything:

message = 'café — 日本語 — Ολα καλά'
print(message)
print(len(message))

π = 3.14159                      # identifiers may be non-ASCII too
print(π * 2)

café — 日本語 — Ολα καλά
21
6.28318

Non-ASCII identifiers are legal and are almost always a bad idea in shared code — they are hard to type and easy to confuse with lookalike characters — but non-ASCII text in strings is entirely normal and needs no declaration.

You will occasionally see this line at the top of old files:

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-

That was required in Python 2, where the default was ASCII. In Python 3 it is redundant. A declaration is only needed if a file is genuinely not UTF-8, which in new code it never should be.

§10.5 covers the related and much more important question of the encoding of files your program reads, where the default is not UTF-8 and where being explicit genuinely matters.

1.6 Comments

A # begins a comment, which runs to the end of the line and is ignored entirely:

# This whole line is a comment.
total = 10 * 3          # so is this, from the hash onwards
print(total)            # print(total * 2) — commented-out code

# There is no block comment syntax in Python.
# Several lines each need their own hash.
print('done')

30
done

Python has no /* ... */. A triple-quoted string on its own line is sometimes used as one, and it is not a comment — it is a string expression that is evaluated and discarded, which mostly does not matter but is worth knowing.

Comment the why, not the what. # add 1 to i restates the code and will go stale; # the API numbers pages from 1 explains something the code cannot. A comment that has drifted out of date with the code is worse than no comment at all, because it is believed.

1.7 Three Errors You Will Meet Today

Errors in Python are informative if you read them, and read them properly means bottom-up and completely (§9.2). Here are the three you will hit first.

A SyntaxError means the file did not even start running.

$ cat syn.py
print("hi"

$ python3 syn.py
  File "syn.py", line 1
    print("hi"
         ^
SyntaxError: '(' was never closed

Nothing at all was executed. The message names the exact problem — an unclosed bracket — and the caret points at it. When a syntax error points at a line that looks perfectly fine, look at the line above: an unclosed bracket or quote makes the parser read the next line as a continuation of this one.

A NameError means you used a name that does not exist.

$ cat nam.py
x = 1
print(y)

$ python3 nam.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "nam.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(y)
          ^
NameError: name 'y' is not defined

Note that x = 1 did run — this is a runtime error, so everything before it happened. The cause is nearly always a typo, or using a name before assigning it.

An IndentationError means the whitespace is inconsistent. Python uses indentation to define blocks, so it has to be exact:

$ cat ind.py
def greet():
print('hello')

$ python3 ind.py
  File "ind.py", line 2
    print('hello')
    ^
IndentationError: expected an indented block after function definition on line 1

The rules: indent with four spaces, never tabs, and never a mixture. Every editor can be told to insert spaces when you press Tab, and doing that once will save you from a category of error that is invisible on screen.

Errors are not a sign that you are doing badly. Reading them carefully is the single highest-return habit in this section, and §9 covers the whole system properly once you have written enough code to hit it.

1.8 An Editor

You can write Python in any text editor. What you want from one is four things, all of which the common choices give you:

syntax highlighting
Colours strings, keywords and comments. An unterminated string becomes visible instantly.
spaces for Tab
Set it to insert four spaces. This removes §1.7's IndentationError class of bug.
a linter
Underlines undefined names, unused imports and typos as you type (§14.8).
an integrated terminal
So running the file is one keystroke, not a window switch.

VS Code with the Python extension is the common default and is free; PyCharm is the heavyweight alternative; Vim, Emacs and Neovim all work well with a language server. The choice matters far less than the four settings above. What genuinely does not work is a word processor — it will insert curly quotes and non-breaking spaces that Python cannot parse.

1.9 A Project Directory, and an Environment

You do not need this for the first few sections, and you will need it before you install anything. §12.8 explains the mechanism; here is the recipe.

mkdir -p ~/python-foundations
cd ~/python-foundations
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install --upgrade pip

$ python3 -m venv .venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ which python3
/home/ada/python-foundations/.venv/bin/python3
(.venv) $ python3 -m pip install ruff
Successfully installed ruff-0.16.4
(.venv) $ deactivate
$ which python3
/usr/bin/python3

On Windows the activation command is .venv\Scripts\activate instead.

The (.venv) in the prompt tells you it is active. Everything you install while it is active goes into that directory and nowhere else, so a project cannot break another one, and deleting .venv undoes everything. Activation lasts until you close the terminal.

Three habits worth forming now:

One .venv per project, in the project directory, named .venv so editors find it.

Never install into the system Python. On many Linux distributions pip install outside an environment now refuses outright, precisely because doing it can break the operating system's own tools.

When something is "installed but not found", ask which Python is running. which python3 and python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)" answer the question in one line each, and answer it correctly more often than memory does.

1.10 The Loop You Will Actually Work In

Put together, the working cycle is short and you will repeat it thousands of times:

1
Write or change a few lines in the editor. A few — not fifty.
2
Run it: python3 script.py.
3
Read what happened — the output, or the error, all of it.
4
If something is unclear, try it in the REPL in isolation.
5
Repeat.

The mistake almost every beginner makes is writing thirty lines before running anything, then facing an error with thirty candidate causes. Run after every few lines. When a program is working after each change, a break is caused by the change you just made, and you have narrowed it to a handful of lines for free.

print is your instrument for step 3, and it is a legitimate one — §14.2 shows how to use it well and §14.3 introduces a debugger for when it is not enough.

Two more things that will save you time. Keep a scratch file — scratch.py — for trying things out, so experiments do not accumulate in real code. And type the examples in this course rather than copying them. Typing them surfaces the small errors that copying hides, and every one of those errors is something you will otherwise meet later under worse conditions.

Exercises

Exercise 1.1 — Diagnose four failures. For each, say what went wrong and how to fix it.

(a) $ python3 hello.py
    python3: can't open file '/home/ada/hello.py': [Errno 2] No such file or directory

(b) $ python3 script.py
      File "script.py", line 4
        print(total)
        ^
    IndentationError: unexpected indent

(c) $ python3 -c "print(2+2)"
    4
    $ python script.py
    Command 'python' not found

(d) $ python3 -m pip install requests
    Successfully installed requests-2.32.4
    $ python3 -c "import requests"
    ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requests'
Solution

(a) You are in the wrong directory. Python resolves a relative filename against the current working directory, and the message prints the full path it tried — /home/ada/hello.py. Compare that with where the file actually is. ls to see what is here, pwd to see where "here" is, then cd to the right place or give the path: python3 projects/first-steps/hello.py.

(b) The indentation is inconsistent. "Unexpected indent" means line 4 is indented where nothing opened a block — usually a stray space or tab at the start, or a line accidentally pushed in while editing. Check that the file uses four spaces and no tabs; most editors have a "show whitespace" or "convert indentation to spaces" command that makes this visible and fixable in one step.

(c) python and python3 are different commands. On most systems only python3 exists; python was Python 2 and has been removed. Always type python3, and inside an activated virtual environment python will also work because the environment provides it. If you would rather not type the 3, an alias is fine — but keep using python3 in anything you share.

(d) Two different interpreters. The install went to whichever Python python3 was at that moment, and the import ran in a different one — the usual cause is that a virtual environment was activated for one command and not the other, or a new terminal was opened in between. Diagnose it in one line each:

python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.executable); print(sys.prefix)"
python3 -m pip --version

pip --version prints the interpreter it installs for. If those two disagree, that is the whole answer. Activate the environment and re-run both.

The pattern across all four: the error message contains the diagnosis. The path it tried, the line it objected to, the command it could not find, the module it could not import. Reading it completely — rather than pattern-matching on the last word and guessing — resolves most of them without any other information.

Exercise 1.2 — Set up and prove it. Create a project directory with a virtual environment, write a script that reports which interpreter is running, and verify it behaves differently inside and outside the environment.

Solution

The script needs nothing but sys:

import sys
from pathlib import Path

print(f'executable : {Path(sys.executable).name}')
print(f'version    : {".".join(str(n) for n in sys.version_info[:2])}')
print(f'in a venv  : {sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix}')
print(f'path[0] is the script dir : {len(sys.path) > 0}')

executable : python3.14
version    : 3.14
in a venv  : False
path[0] is the script dir : True

The key line is sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix. sys.base_prefix always points at the underlying installation; sys.prefix points at the active environment. Outside a virtual environment they are identical, and inside one they differ — which is the official way to detect an active environment, and is more reliable than checking for a VIRTUAL_ENV variable that a user could set by hand.

The full session:

$ mkdir -p ~/python-foundations && cd ~/python-foundations
$ python3 -m venv .venv

$ python3 whichpy.py
executable : python3
version    : 3.14
in a venv  : False

$ source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ python3 whichpy.py
executable : python3
version    : 3.14
in a venv  : True

(.venv) $ python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"
/home/ada/python-foundations/.venv
(.venv) $ deactivate
$ python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"
/usr/

Same file, same command, different answer — because activate put .venv/bin at the front of PATH and nothing else (§12.8).

Keep this script. "Which Python am I running, and is my environment active?" is the first question to ask whenever an import fails or a package seems to have vanished, and having the answer in one command is worth the four lines.

Exercise 1.3 — REPL or script? For each task, say which you would use and why. Then check the two claims marked with a question in a REPL.

(a) Working out whether str.split() keeps empty strings.
(b) A program that renames a thousand files.
(c) Checking what round(2.675, 2) gives.
(d) Anything you will run more than twice.
(e) Exploring what methods a dict has.
Solution

(a), (c) and (e) are REPL work. Each is a single question with a single answer, and the cost of finding out is one line. Writing a file, saving it and running it to learn what split does is four times the work for the same information.

(b) and (d) are scripts. Anything with more than a few lines, anything you will run again, and anything with a consequence — renaming a thousand files certainly qualifies — belongs in a file where it can be read, reviewed, corrected and re-run.

The dividing line is whether you want to keep it. The REPL has no history you can trust, no way to fix line three after typing line ten, and nothing to show a colleague.

Here are the two checks, in the REPL where they belong:

$ python3
>>> '  a  b  '.split()
['a', 'b']
>>> '  a  b  '.split(' ')
['', '', 'a', '', 'b', '', '']
>>> 'a,,b'.split(',')
['a', '', 'b']
>>> round(2.675, 2)
2.67

split() with no argument discards empties; split(sep) keeps them. That is not an inconsistency — the bare form means "split on runs of whitespace", which has no notion of an empty field, while an explicit separator means "cut here, every time" (§5.5).

round(2.675, 2) gives 2.67, not 2.68. The stored float is very slightly less than 2.675, so the nearest two-decimal value really is 2.67 (§2.5). Both of these are things you would be quite likely to state wrongly from memory, and both took under ten seconds to settle — which is the entire argument for having a REPL open while you work.

And for (e):

>>> [m for m in dir(dict) if not m.startswith('_')]
['clear', 'copy', 'fromkeys', 'get', 'items', 'keys', 'pop', 'popitem', 'setdefault', 'update', 'values']
>>> help(dict.setdefault)

dir() for the list, help() for what one of them does. Between them they answer most "how do I…" questions faster than a search engine, and they answer them for the exact version you are running rather than for whatever version the top result was written against.

SECTION 2

Values, Names and Types

Everything a Python program manipulates is an object: a number, a piece of text, a list, a function, a module. Every object has a type that determines what it can do, and every name in your program is a label attached to one. Getting those two ideas straight — objects have types, names are labels — dissolves most of the confusion that beginners have about assignment, copying and equality, and it is the foundation the rest of this course is built on.

2.1 Names Are Labels, Not Boxes

Most introductions say a variable is a box that holds a value. In Python that model is wrong, and it will mislead you within a week.

A name is a label tied to an object. Assignment does not put a value into a container; it points a label at an object.

x = 42
y = x

print(x, y)
print(id(x) == id(y))          # the same object, not a copy

42 42
True

id() returns an object's identity — in CPython, its address in memory. x and y name the same 42.

Rebinding a name moves the label. It does not affect any other label:

x = 42
y = x
x = 99                          # x now points somewhere else

print(x, y)

99 42

So far the box model would have given the same answer. The difference shows the moment the object can be changed:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
a.append(4)                     # changes the OBJECT, not the label

print(a, b)
print(a is b)

[1, 2, 3, 4] [1, 2, 3, 4]
True

b was never assigned again, and b changed. Under the box model that is inexplicable. Under the label model it is obvious: there was one list and two labels on it, and the list was modified.

assignment
a = … points the label a at an object. Nothing else is affected, ever.
mutation
a.append(…), a[0] = …, a.sort() change the object itself. Every label on it sees the change.

That single distinction explains the mutable-default-argument trap (§4.3), the shared class attribute (§11.4), the aliased grid (§6.4) and the function that unexpectedly modifies its caller's list (§4.8). They are all the same thing seen from four angles.

Several names can be assigned at once, and the right-hand side is fully evaluated first:

a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a                     # a genuine swap, no temporary needed
print(a, b)

x = y = z = 0                   # all three label the same object
print(x, y, z, x is y)

2 1
0 0 0 True

Names must start with a letter or underscore, may contain letters, digits and underscores, and are case-sensitive. The convention is lower_snake_case for variables and functions, CapWords for classes, and UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants — which Python does not enforce, since it has no constants, but which every reader relies on.

2.2 Types

Every object has a type, and type() reports it:

for value in [42, 3.14, 'text', True, None, [1], (1,), {1}, {'a': 1}]:
    print(f'{value!r:10} {type(value).__name__}')

42         int
3.14       float
'text'     str
True       bool
None       NoneType
[1]        list
(1,)       tuple
{1}        set
{'a': 1}   dict

The type belongs to the object, not to the name. A name can be pointed at anything, and then at something else:

x = 42
print(type(x).__name__)
x = 'now a string'
print(type(x).__name__)

int
str

That is what "dynamically typed" means. It is convenient and it is also why type hints (§14.7) exist: nothing stops you from putting a string where the rest of the program expects a number, and the failure appears later, somewhere else.

Python is nevertheless strongly typed — it does not silently convert between unrelated types:

try:
    print('5' + 5)
except TypeError as e:
    print(f'TypeError: {e}')

print('5' * 3)                  # this IS defined: repetition
print(5 * 3)

TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
555
15

'5' + 5 is an error rather than '55' or 10, because Python refuses to guess which you meant. Note that '5' * 3 is perfectly legal and means something else entirely — a source of confusion when a number arrives from a file or input() as a string.

Use isinstance rather than type(x) == ... when you need to test a type, because it also accepts subclasses:

print(isinstance(42, int), isinstance(True, int))
print(type(True) == int)
print(isinstance(3.0, (int, float)))

True True
False
True

True really is an int — §2.6 explains why — and isinstance is the check that knows it.

2.3 Integers

Python integers have no maximum size. They grow to fit, limited only by memory:

print(2 ** 10)
print(2 ** 100)
print(len(str(2 ** 1000)))
print(9_999_999_999_999_999_999 + 1)

1024
1267650600228229401496703205376
302
10000000000000000000

That is unusual and genuinely useful: there is no integer overflow in Python, so a factorial or a hash never silently wraps around. Underscores may be used as digit separators in a literal — 1_000_000 is 1000000 — purely for readability.

Integers can be written in other bases, and converted back:

print(0b1010, 0o17, 0xff)
print(bin(10), oct(15), hex(255))
print(int('ff', 16), int('1010', 2))

10 15 255
0b1010 0o17 0xff
255 10

2.4 Arithmetic, and the Two Divisions

print(7 + 3, 7 - 3, 7 * 3)
print(7 / 3)                    # true division: ALWAYS a float
print(7 // 3)                   # floor division: rounds DOWN
print(7 % 3)                    # remainder
print(7 ** 3)                   # power
print(divmod(7, 3))

10 4 21
2.3333333333333335
2
1
343
(2, 1)

/ always produces a float, even when the division is exact. That trips people up constantly:

print(6 / 3, type(6 / 3).__name__)
print(6 // 3, type(6 // 3).__name__)

2.0 float
2 int

If you need an integer index or count, use //. If you use / and then index with the result, you get TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not float.

Floor division rounds towards negative infinity, not towards zero, and % follows it:

print(7 // 2, -7 // 2)
print(7 % 3, -7 % 3)
print(int(-7 / 2))              # int() truncates towards zero instead

3 -4
1 2
-3

-7 // 2 is -4, not -3. The compensating property is that a == (a // b) * b + a % b holds for negatives too, and that % always returns a result with the sign of the divisor — so -1 % 12 is 11, which is exactly what you want for clock arithmetic and wrapping indices.

Operator precedence follows the usual mathematical rules — ** first, then unary minus, then *, /, //, %, then + and -. When in doubt, parenthesise; nobody has ever complained about a bracket that made an expression clearer.

print(2 + 3 * 4)
print((2 + 3) * 4)
print(-2 ** 2)                  # ** binds tighter than unary minus
print((-2) ** 2)

14
20
-4
4

2.5 Floats and Representation Error

A float is a binary approximation of a real number, stored in 64 bits of floating-point format — the IEEE 754 double that every mainstream language uses. Most decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly in binary, exactly as one third cannot be written exactly in decimal.

print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(f'{0.1:.20f}')
print(1.0, type(1.0).__name__, 1e3, 1.5e-4)

0.30000000000000004
False
0.10000000000000000555
1.0 float 1000.0 0.00015

That is not a bug in Python: every language with IEEE 754 floating-point behaves identically. 0.1 is stored as the nearest representable binary value, which is very slightly more than a tenth, and the error surfaces when several of them are added.

This is a representation error, and there are three correct responses depending on what you are doing.

Comparing floats: use a tolerance.

import math

print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
print(abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < 1e-9)
print(round(0.1 + 0.2, 10) == round(0.3, 10))

True
True
True

Money: never use floats. Use decimal.Decimal constructed from strings, or store integer cents:

from decimal import Decimal

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.2') == Decimal('0.3'))
print(Decimal(0.1))             # from a float: the error is faithfully copied

False
True
0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625

That last line is the whole argument in one output. §13.4 covers Decimal properly.

Displaying: round at the edge, not in the middle. Compute with full precision and format only when printing (§5.6):

total = 0.0
for _ in range(10):
    total += 0.1                # ten additions, ten small errors

print(total)
print(f'{total:.2f}')
print(round(total, 2))
print(sum([0.1] * 10))          # since 3.12, sum() compensates and gets this exact

0.9999999999999999
1.00
1.0
1.0

That last line is worth knowing about rather than relying on: since Python 3.12 the built-in sum() uses a compensated summation algorithm for floats, so it recovers the exact 1.0 that the hand-written loop above it loses. That is a property of sum, not of floats — the error is still there in every individual addition, and a running total accumulated with += still drifts. Prefer sum() where you can, and do not conclude that float arithmetic has become exact.

One more surprise worth meeting deliberately: round() uses banker's rounding, going to the nearest even number on an exact half. That is a deliberate statistical choice, not a mistake:

print(round(0.5), round(1.5), round(2.5), round(3.5))
print(round(2.675, 2))          # 2.675 is really 2.67499999...

0 2 2 4
2.67

If you need "always round half up" — for money, typically — decimal gives you it explicitly with ROUND_HALF_UP.

2.6 Booleans and None

True and False are the two boolean values, and bool is a subclass of int:

print(True + True, True * 3, int(True), int(False))
print(isinstance(True, int))
print(sum([True, False, True, True]))

2 3 1 0
True
3

That last line is a genuinely useful idiom: sum(...) over a sequence of conditions counts how many are true.

words = ['ada', 'grace', 'al', 'turing']
print(sum(len(w) > 3 for w in words), 'words are longer than 3 characters')

2 words are longer than 3 characters

None is a single object meaning "no value". It is not zero, not the empty string, and not False — though it is falsey (§3.4):

print(None == False, None == 0, None == '')
print(bool(None))
print(None is None)

def f():
    pass
print(f() is None)

False False False
False
True
True

Test for None with is, never with ==. None is a singleton — there is exactly one of it in the interpreter — so identity is the exact question, and == can be redefined by a class in a way that lies.

None is what a function with no return gives back (§4.1), what dict.get returns for a missing key (§7.2), and the conventional "not supplied" default for an optional parameter (§4.3).

2.7 Mutable and Immutable

This is the distinction that decides how a value behaves when it is shared.

Immutable — cannot be changed after creation.
int, float, bool, str, tuple, frozenset, bytes, None
Mutable — can be changed in place.
list, dict, set, bytearray, and most objects you define yourself 
s = 'hello'
try:
    s[0] = 'H'
except TypeError as e:
    print(f'TypeError: {e}')

items = [1, 2, 3]
items[0] = 99                   # a list is mutable
print(items)

TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
[99, 2, 3]

Immutable does not mean the name cannot be reassigned. It means the object cannot be altered:

s = 'hello'
print(id(s) == id(s))
before = id(s)
s = s.upper()                   # a NEW string; the old one is untouched
print(s, id(s) == before)

t = 'hello'
u = t
t += ' world'                   # also a new string
print(t, u)

True
HELLO False
hello world hello

Compare that with the list case from §2.1: t += ' world' left u alone, because strings are immutable and += had to build a new one. The same operator on a list would have mutated it and u would have changed too.

a = [1]
b = a
a += [2]                        # in-place extend for a list
print(a, b, a is b)

c = (1,)
d = c
c += (2,)                       # a new tuple for a tuple
print(c, d, c is d)

[1, 2] [1, 2] True
(1, 2) (1,) False

The same += did two different things, decided entirely by whether the left-hand object is mutable. This is the single most important consequence of the distinction, and §4.8 shows it deciding whether a function can affect its caller.

Immutability is what makes a value hashable and therefore usable as a dictionary key or a set element (§7.4) — a key whose value changed after insertion could never be found again.

2.8 Identity Versus Equality

== asks whether two objects have the same value. is asks whether they are the same object.

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
c = a

print(a == b, a is b)
print(a == c, a is c)
print(a is not b)

True False
True True
True

Two lists with the same contents are equal and are not identical. Getting these confused produces bugs that are hard to see, because is usually happens to give the right answer on small examples:

x = 100
y = 100
print(x == y, x is y)           # both True — by accident

x = 1000
y = 1000
print(x == y, x is y)           # still both True — a different accident

True True
True True

Both printed True is True, and neither is a guarantee. CPython pre-creates the integers −5 to 256, and separately the compiler folds identical constants appearing in one block of code. Change how the same values reach the interpreter and the answer changes:

$ python3
>>> x = 1000
>>> y = 1000
>>> x is y
False
>>> x == y
True

Use is only for None, True, False and sentinel objects. For every other comparison, ==. §3.3 revisits this once you have loops and conditionals to use it in.

2.9 Converting Between Types

Type conversion in Python is explicit: you call the type you want, and it builds a new object of that type from the one you gave it.

print(int('42'), int(3.99), int('1010', 2))
print(float('3.14'), float(7))
print(str(42), str(3.14), str([1, 2]))
print(bool(0), bool('a'), bool([]))
print(list('abc'), tuple([1, 2]), set([1, 1, 2]))

42 3 10
3.14 7.0
42 3.14 [1, 2]
False True False
['a', 'b', 'c'] (1, 2) {1, 2}

int() on a float truncates towards zero — it does not round.

print(int(3.99), int(-3.99))
print(round(3.99), round(-3.99))
import math
print(math.floor(-3.1), math.ceil(-3.1), math.trunc(-3.1))

3 -3
4 -4
-4 -3 -3

Conversion fails loudly when the value does not make sense, which is what you want:

for text in ['42', '3.14', 'forty-two', '', ' 7 ']:
    try:
        print(f'{text!r:12} -> {int(text)}')
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f'{text!r:12} -> ValueError: {e}')

'42'         -> 42
'3.14'       -> ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.14'
'forty-two'  -> ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'forty-two'
''           -> ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: ''
' 7 '        -> 7

Two things there are worth noting. int('3.14') fails — int parses integers, so a decimal string needs int(float(text)). And surrounding whitespace is tolerated, which is convenient when reading a file.

Because type conversion from user input or a file can always fail, the safe-conversion helper is worth writing once and reusing:

def to_int(text, default=None):
    """Convert text to an int, or return default if it cannot be parsed."""
    try:
        return int(text)
    except (ValueError, TypeError):
        return default

print(to_int('42'), to_int('abc'), to_int(None), to_int('abc', 0))

42 None None 0

Catching TypeError as well as ValueError matters: int(None) raises the former, and a value that arrived from a JSON file or a missing dictionary key is exactly the case you are guarding against.

2.10 Augmented Assignment

x += 1 is augmented assignment, and there is one for every arithmetic operator:

n = 10
n += 5;  print(n)
n -= 3;  print(n)
n *= 2;  print(n)
n /= 4;  print(n)               # note: /= produces a float
n //= 2; print(n)
n **= 2; print(n)
n %= 5;  print(n)

15
12
24
6.0
3.0
9.0
4.0

Once /= has been used the value is a float and stays one, which is a small trap in a loop that expects an integer counter.

It works on sequences too, and there the mutable/immutable distinction from §2.7 returns:

s = 'ab'
s += 'cd'                       # new string
print(s)

items = [1]
items += [2]                    # in place, like extend
print(items)

items += 'xy'                   # += on a list takes ANY iterable
print(items)

try:
    items = items + 'xy'        # + does not
except TypeError as e:
    print(f'TypeError: {e}')

abcd
[1, 2]
[1, 2, 'x', 'y']
TypeError: can only concatenate list (not "str") to list

items += 'xy' and items = items + 'xy' are not the same operation — the first is extend, the second is +, and only the first accepts a string. Prefer items.append(x) or items.extend(other), which say which one you mean.

Python has no ++ or --. n++ is a syntax error and ++n silently means "positive positive n", which is just n:

n = 5
print(++n, --n, +-n)

5 5 -5

That prints numbers rather than raising, which is exactly why the operators were left out: ++n looks like an increment and is not one.

2.11 Getting Input

input() reads one line from the user and always returns a string, with the trailing newline removed:

$ cat greet.py
name = input('What is your name? ')
age = input('How old are you? ')
print(f'Hello, {name}. Next year you will be {int(age) + 1}.')
print(type(name).__name__, type(age).__name__)

$ python3 greet.py
What is your name? Ada
How old are you? 36
Hello, Ada. Next year you will be 37.
str str

The conversion is not optional. age + 1 would raise TypeError, and age * 2 would produce '3636' rather than 72 — the §2.2 trap, arriving through the front door.

Anything a user types can be nonsense, so a real prompt loop validates and re-asks:

$ cat ask.py
def ask_int(prompt):
    while True:
        raw = input(prompt).strip()
        try:
            return int(raw)
        except ValueError:
            print(f'  {raw!r} is not a whole number — try again')

age = ask_int('How old are you? ')
print(f'You are {age}.')

$ printf 'twelve\n\n12\n' | python3 ask.py
How old are you?   'twelve' is not a whole number — try again
How old are you?   '' is not a whole number — try again
How old are you? You are 12.

That shape — while True, try to parse, return on success, explain and loop on failure — is the standard one, and §3.5 covers the loop and §9.4 the try.

For anything beyond a toy, prefer arguments over prompts: a program reading sys.argv or using argparse (§13.8) can be scripted, tested and run unattended, and one that stops to ask questions cannot.

Exercises

Exercise 2.1 — Predict ten. Say what each prints and why.

print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, -7 // 2)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(int('3.0') if False else int(float('3.0')))
print(True + True, isinstance(True, int))
print('5' * 3, 5 * 3)
a = [1]; b = a; a += [2]
c = (1,); d = c; c += (2,)
print(a, b, c, d)
print(round(0.5), round(1.5))
print(None == False)
Solution 
print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, -7 // 2)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(int(float('3.0')))
print(True + True, isinstance(True, int))
print('5' * 3, 5 * 3)
a = [1]; b = a; a += [2]
c = (1,); d = c; c += (2,)
print(a, b, c, d)
print(round(0.5), round(1.5))
print(None == False)

3.5 3 -4
False
3
2 True
555 15
[1, 2] [1, 2] (1, 2) (1,)
0 2
False

7 / 2 is 3.5 — true division always gives a float. -7 // 2 is -4, because floor division rounds towards negative infinity rather than towards zero.

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False — representation error (§2.5). Use math.isclose.

int(float('3.0')) is 3. int('3.0') would raise, because int parses integers and '3.0' is not one.

True + True is 2 — bool is a subclass of int, so isinstance(True, int) is True too.

'5' * 3 is '555' — string repetition, not arithmetic. This is what makes forgetting to convert input() so insidious: it does not always raise.

a and b both show [1, 2]; c shows (1, 2) and d shows (1,). The same += mutated the list in place (so both labels see it) and built a new tuple (so only c moved). This is §2.7's point and the one worth being able to explain out loud.

round(0.5) is 0 and round(1.5) is 2 — banker's rounding, going to the nearest even number on an exact half.

None == False is False. None is falsey, which is not the same as being equal to False (§3.4 makes the same point about []).

Exercise 2.2 — Fix the price calculator. This has four defects. Find them all, explain what each one does wrong, and rewrite.

def receipt(item, price, qty, discount):
    subtotal = price * qty
    if discount != None:
        subtotal = subtotal - subtotal * discount / 100
    tax = subtotal * 0.2
    total = subtotal + tax
    return item + ': ' + total
Solution

1. discount != None should be discount is not None (§2.6). None is a singleton and identity is the exact question; == can be redefined by a class and is slower.

2. item + ': ' + total concatenates a string and a float, which raises TypeError (§2.2). The fix is an f-string, which converts and formats in one step.

3. Money is being computed in floats (§2.5). 19.99 * 3 is not exactly 59.97, and after a percentage discount and a tax multiplication the error compounds. Prices should be Decimal built from strings, or integer pence.

4. There is no validation. A negative quantity, a discount of 150%, or a price that arrived from input() as a string all produce a confident, wrong answer rather than an error.

Here is the failure demonstrated before it is fixed:

def receipt(item, price, qty, discount):
    subtotal = price * qty
    if discount != None:
        subtotal = subtotal - subtotal * discount / 100
    tax = subtotal * 0.2
    total = subtotal + tax
    return item + ': ' + total

try:
    print(receipt('book', 19.99, 3, None))
except TypeError as e:
    print(f'TypeError: {e}')

print(19.99 * 3)                       # the float problem, on its own
print(19.99 * 3 * 1.2)

TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "float") to str
59.97
71.964

19.99 * 3 looks right, and * 1.2 gives 71.964 where exact decimal arithmetic gives 71.964 too — the errors are small until they are summed over ten thousand line items and compared against a bank statement.

The rewrite:

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

TAX_RATE = Decimal('0.20')
PENNY = Decimal('0.01')

def receipt(item, price, qty, discount=None):
    """Return a formatted receipt line. price is a decimal string; discount is a percentage."""
    if qty < 1:
        raise ValueError(f'quantity must be at least 1, got {qty}')
    if discount is not None and not 0 <= discount <= 100:
        raise ValueError(f'discount must be between 0 and 100, got {discount}')

    subtotal = Decimal(str(price)) * qty
    if discount is not None:
        subtotal -= subtotal * Decimal(str(discount)) / 100
    total = (subtotal * (1 + TAX_RATE)).quantize(PENNY, rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
    return f'{item}: {total}'

print(receipt('book', '19.99', 3))
print(receipt('book', '19.99', 3, discount=10))
print(receipt('pen', '0.01', 7))

for bad in [{'qty': 0}, {'qty': 1, 'discount': 150}]:
    try:
        receipt('x', '1.00', **bad)
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f'ValueError: {e}')

book: 71.96
book: 64.77
pen: 0.08
ValueError: quantity must be at least 1, got 0
ValueError: discount must be between 0 and 100, got 150

Four fixes and one bonus. The bonus is quantize(PENNY, ROUND_HALF_UP): rounding happens once, at the end, to the nearest penny, using the rounding rule a customer expects rather than the banker's rounding round() would apply (§2.5). Rounding at each intermediate step instead is a classic way to lose a penny per line item.

Decimal(str(price)) accepts either a string or a number and never inherits a float's error — Decimal(19.99) would (§2.5).

Exercise 2.3 — Explain the mystery. normalise is supposed to return a cleaned copy and leave its input alone. Explain precisely why it does not, and give two fixes with different trade-offs.

def normalise(record):
    record['name'] = record['name'].strip().title()
    record['tags'].append('processed')
    return record

original = {'name': '  ada lovelace ', 'tags': ['maths']}
Solution 
def normalise(record):
    record['name'] = record['name'].strip().title()
    record['tags'].append('processed')
    return record

original = {'name': '  ada lovelace ', 'tags': ['maths']}
cleaned = normalise(original)

print(cleaned)
print(original)
print(cleaned is original)

{'name': 'Ada Lovelace', 'tags': ['maths', 'processed']}
{'name': 'Ada Lovelace', 'tags': ['maths', 'processed']}
True

original was modified, and cleaned is not a copy — it is the same object.

The reason is §2.1 exactly. record is a second label on the caller's dictionary; the function never made anything new. record['name'] = ... is a mutation of the dictionary even though it looks like an assignment — the assignment is to a key, not to the name record. And .append mutates the list. Returning record returns the caller's own object, so cleaned is original.

Note what would not have caused this: record = {...} inside the function would rebind the local label and leave the caller untouched. It is subscript assignment and method calls that reach through.

Fix one — copy first. Simple, and works for any caller.

import copy

def normalise(record):
    record = copy.deepcopy(record)          # a private copy, nested lists included
    record['name'] = record['name'].strip().title()
    record['tags'].append('processed')
    return record

original = {'name': '  ada lovelace ', 'tags': ['maths']}
cleaned = normalise(original)
print(cleaned)
print(original)
print(cleaned is original, cleaned['tags'] is original['tags'])

{'name': 'Ada Lovelace', 'tags': ['maths', 'processed']}
{'name': '  ada lovelace ', 'tags': ['maths']}
False False

deepcopy, not dict(record). A shallow copy would give a new outer dictionary sharing the same tags list (§6.4), so the append would still reach the caller — the fix would appear to work and would fail on exactly the nested case it was written for.

Fix two — build a new value and never mutate anything. More code, and much easier to reason about.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field, replace

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Record:
    name: str
    tags: tuple[str, ...] = ()

def normalise(record):
    return replace(record,
                   name=record.name.strip().title(),
                   tags=record.tags + ('processed',))

original = Record('  ada lovelace ', ('maths',))
cleaned = normalise(original)
print(cleaned)
print(original)
try:
    cleaned.name = 'x'
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)

Record(name='Ada Lovelace', tags=('maths', 'processed'))
Record(name='  ada lovelace ', tags=('maths',))
FrozenInstanceError

The trade-off. Fix one keeps the flexible dictionary and pays a copy on every call — fine for small records, wasteful for large ones, and it still relies on the author remembering to copy. Fix two makes the mutation impossible: frozen=True and a tuple of tags mean there is no operation that could modify the original, so the bug cannot be reintroduced by a later edit (§11.12).

The general rule this exercise is really about: a function should either mutate its argument or return a new value, and its name should say which. normalise sounds like it returns something; add_processed_tag(record) sounds like it mutates. A function doing both, silently, is the one that produces a bug report six months later.

SECTION 3

Control Flow

Everything a program does beyond a straight run of statements comes from three ideas: choosing between paths, repeating work, and stopping early. Python spells them if, for, while, break and continue, plus two constructs — the else clause on a loop and the match statement — that most languages do not have. This section covers all of them, and the truthiness rules that decide what "true" means when the thing being tested is not a boolean.

3.1 if, elif, else

def describe(n):
    if n < 0:
        return 'negative'
    elif n == 0:
        return 'zero'
    elif n < 10:
        return 'small'
    else:
        return 'large'

for n in [-5, 0, 3, 100]:
    print(n, '->', describe(n))

-5 -> negative
0 -> zero
3 -> small
100 -> large

Three mechanical points. Indentation defines the block — there are no braces, and the colon at the end of the condition is required. elif is one word, and there may be any number of them. At most one branch runs: the first whose condition is true, and then the whole statement is finished, which is why describe(-5) never reaches the n < 10 test.

Conditions nest, and nesting more than two deep is usually a sign to restructure:

def access(user):
    if user is None:
        return 'anonymous'
    if not user.get('active'):
        return 'suspended'
    if user.get('admin'):
        return 'admin'
    return 'member'

for u in [None, {'active': False}, {'active': True, 'admin': True}, {'active': True}]:
    print(access(u))

anonymous
suspended
admin
member

That shape — guard clauses, each handling one case and returning immediately — is almost always clearer than a nested if/else pyramid, because each condition is read against nothing and the happy path ends up at the bottom, unindented.

There is also a conditional expression, which chooses a value rather than a path:

n = 7
label = 'even' if n % 2 == 0 else 'odd'
print(label)

items = []
print(f'{len(items)} item{"" if len(items) == 1 else "s"}')

print(max(3, 5) if True else 0)

odd
0 items
5

The order reads oddly at first — value, condition, other value — and it is worth using only when it fits on one line. Chained conditional expressions are legal and unreadable.

3.2 Comparison Operators and Boolean Operators

print(3 == 3.0, 3 != 4, 3 < 4, 3 >= 3)
print('abc' < 'abd', 'Z' < 'a')
print([1, 2] < [1, 3], (1, 2) == (1, 2))
print(3 == '3')

True True True True
True True
True True
False

Those six — ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= — are the comparison operators, and every one of them returns a boolean. Strings compare by code point, left to right, which is why every uppercase letter sorts before every lowercase one. Sequences compare element by element, using the same rule as a dictionary: the first difference decides.

Comparisons can be chained, which is a genuinely nice piece of syntax:

n = 5
print(0 < n < 10)
print(0 < n and n < 10)              # the same thing
print(1 == 1 == 1)

low, high = 3, 8
print(low <= n <= high)

True
True
True
True

Chaining works for any run of comparison operators, and 0 < n < 10 evaluates n once — which matters when n is a function call rather than a variable.

Comparing incompatible types raises rather than guessing:

try:
    3 < 'abc'
except TypeError as e:
    print(f'TypeError: {e}')
print(3 == 'abc')                    # == never raises; it just says False

TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'
False

== is defined for every pair of types and returns False when they are not comparable; the ordering operators are not.

3.3 is Versus ==

== asks whether two objects are equal. is asks whether they are the same object.

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
c = a

print(a == b, a is b)
print(a == c, a is c)
print(id(a) == id(c))

True False
True True
True

a and b look the same and are two separate lists. c is another name for a.

Use is only for None, True and False, which are singletons — there is exactly one of each in the whole interpreter:

x = None
print(x is None, x == None)          # both True; the first is the correct spelling

def f(value=None):
    if value is None:                # right
        return 'default'
    return value

print(f(), f(0), f(''))

True True
default 0

Why is None rather than == None: == can be overridden by a class, so an object could define equality that claims to equal None. is cannot be fooled. The same applies to sentinel objects (§9.11's MISSING).

Small integers and short strings produce a confusing result that is worth understanding once and then ignoring:

a, b = 256, 256
print(a is b)
c, d = 257, 257
print(c is d)
e, f = 'hello', 'hello'
print(e is f)

True
True
True

Every one of those is True, and not one of them is guaranteed to be. CPython pre-creates the integers −5 to 256, interns short strings that look like identifiers, and folds identical constants within a single compiled block — so c is d is True here and is False if the two 257s are typed on separate lines of an interactive session:

$ python3
>>> c = 257
>>> d = 257
>>> c is d
False
>>> c == d
True

Same values, same expression, opposite answers, depending only on how the code was compiled. These are implementation details, not language rules, and depending on any of them is a bug. Never use is to compare numbers or strings — use ==.

3.4 Truthiness

Any object can be used where a boolean is expected. The rule is short: empty is false, zero is false, None is false, everything else is true.

for value in [0, 1, -1, 0.0, '', 'a', ' ', [], [0], {}, {'a': 1}, set(), None]:
    print(f'{value!r:10} {bool(value)}')

0          False
1          True
-1         True
0.0        False
''         False
'a'        True
' '        True
[]         False
[0]        True
{}         False
{'a': 1}   True
set()      False
None       False

Note that the empty set() is falsey along with the empty list and the empty dictionary — set() is the way to write it, since {} is an empty dictionary (§7.8). Two entries deserve attention. ' ' — a string containing a space — is true, because it is not empty. And [0] is true, because it is a list with one item in it; the item's own truthiness is irrelevant.

This makes the idiomatic emptiness check very short:

items = []
if not items:
    print('nothing to do')

name = ''
print(name or 'anonymous')           # `or` returns the first truthy operand
print('Ada' or 'anonymous')
print(0 or 42, None or 0 or 'last')
print('a' and 'b', '' and 'b')

nothing to do
anonymous
Ada
42 last
b

The boolean operators are and, or and not. The first two do not return booleans — they return one of their operands, and they short-circuit, evaluating the right-hand side only if they must. That is what makes value or default work, and what makes this guard safe:

def head(items):
    return items and items[0]        # items[0] is never reached when items is empty

print(head([1, 2]), repr(head([])))

config = {}
port = config.get('port') or 8080    # falls back on missing AND on 0
print(port)

1 []
8080

The or default has one trap, visible in that last line: it also replaces a legitimate zero or empty string. If config['port'] were genuinely 0, this would silently use 8080. When the falsey value is meaningful, test for None explicitly:

config = {'port': 0, 'name': ''}

print(config.get('port') or 8080)                        # wrong: 0 is meaningful
print(config.get('port') if config.get('port') is not None else 8080)
print(config.get('name', 'default'), repr(config.get('name')))

8080
0
 ''

One more rule: compare to None and to sentinels with is, but do not compare to True and False at all.

flag = 1
print(flag == True, flag is True, bool(flag))
if flag:                             # the correct spelling
    print('truthy')

True False True
truthy

if x == True: is redundant and gives the wrong answer for anything that is truthy without being True. if x: is shorter and correct.

3.5 while

while repeats as long as a condition holds:

n = 5
while n > 0:
    print(n, end=' ')
    n -= 1
print('liftoff')

5 4 3 2 1 liftoff

The condition is checked before each pass, so a loop whose condition is false at the start runs zero times.

A while loop is the right choice when the number of repetitions is not known in advance — reading until end of input, retrying until success, converging on an answer:

def collatz_steps(n):
    """How many steps to reach 1?"""
    steps = 0
    while n != 1:
        n = n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1
        steps += 1
    return steps

print([collatz_steps(n) for n in [1, 6, 27]])

[0, 8, 111]

while True with a break is the standard shape for "loop until something happens", especially around input:

$ cat menu.py
while True:
    choice = input('> ').strip().lower()
    if choice in ('q', 'quit'):
        print('bye')
        break
    if not choice:
        continue
    print(f'you said {choice!r}')

$ printf 'hello\n\nquit\n' | python3 menu.py
> you said 'hello'
> > bye

Every while loop needs something that eventually makes the condition false. Forget it and the program hangs — no error, no output, just a process to kill. The three usual causes are forgetting to change the variable, changing the wrong one, and a condition that can be skipped over (while n != 10 where n increases by 3).

3.6 for and range

for iterates over the items of any iterable (§8.1):

for colour in ['red', 'green']:
    print(colour, end=' ')
print()

for ch in 'abc':
    print(ch, end=' ')
print()

for key in {'a': 1, 'b': 2}:
    print(key, end=' ')
print()

for i in range(3):
    print(i, end=' ')
print()

red green 
a b c 
a b 
0 1 2

range() produces a sequence of integers, and its three forms mirror slicing. range(stop), range(start, stop) and range(start, stop, step) are the whole interface:

print(list(range(5)))
print(list(range(2, 6)))
print(list(range(0, 10, 3)))
print(list(range(5, 0, -1)))
print(list(range(5, 5)))
print(range(1_000_000))

[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
[2, 3, 4, 5]
[0, 3, 6, 9]
[5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
[]
range(0, 1000000)

A range() object is lazy — the last line shows it printing as itself rather than as a million numbers — so range(10**9) costs nothing until you iterate it. The stop value is exclusive, exactly as in slicing, so range(5) gives five numbers starting at zero.

Do not write for i in range(len(items)) to visit items. enumerate (§8.6) is the tool when you need the index, and a plain for item in items when you do not:

items = ['a', 'b', 'c']

for i in range(len(items)):          # C-style; avoid
    print(i, items[i], end='  ')
print()

for i, item in enumerate(items):     # Pythonic
    print(i, item, end='  ')
print()

0 a  1 b  2 c  
0 a  1 b  2 c

range(len(...)) is legitimate in exactly one situation: when you need the index but not the item, such as building a list of the same length.

3.7 break, continue and pass

break leaves the loop entirely. continue skips to the next iteration. The pass statement does nothing at all and exists so that a block can be syntactically present but empty.

for n in range(10):
    if n == 3:
        continue                     # skip 3
    if n == 6:
        break                        # stop entirely
    print(n, end=' ')
print()

for n in range(3):
    pass                             # a placeholder, so this parses
print('done')

def not_written_yet():
    pass
print(not_written_yet())

0 1 2 4 5 
done
None

A pass statement is needed wherever Python's grammar demands an indented block and you have nothing to put in it — a function you have not written yet, an exception class whose body is empty (§9.8), a branch you are deliberately ignoring. ... (the Ellipsis literal) is sometimes used the same way and means the same thing to the interpreter.

break and continue affect only the innermost loop. Escaping two loops needs a flag, a function with a return, or an exception:

matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]

found = None
for row in matrix:
    for value in row:
        if value == 4:
            found = value
            break                    # leaves the inner loop only
    if found is not None:
        break                        # ...so an outer break is needed too
print(found)

def find(matrix, target):
    for row in matrix:
        for value in row:
            if value == target:
                return value         # leaves both loops at once
    return None

print(find(matrix, 4), find(matrix, 99))

4
4 None

Wrapping a search in a function and using return is the cleanest escape from nested loops, and it usually improves the code for other reasons too.

3.8 else on a Loop

Python lets a loop have an else clause — the loop else — which runs only if the loop finished without hitting break. It is unusual, the name is confusing, and it is exactly right for search loops.

def find_first_even(numbers):
    for n in numbers:
        if n % 2 == 0:
            print(f'found {n}')
            break
    else:
        print('no even number')

find_first_even([1, 3, 4, 5])
find_first_even([1, 3, 5])
find_first_even([])

found 4
no even number
no even number

Read the loop else as "if no break" and it stops being confusing. Without it, the same logic needs a flag:

def find_first_even(numbers):
    found = False
    for n in numbers:
        if n % 2 == 0:
            found = True
            break
    if not found:
        print('no even number')
    else:
        print(f'found {n}')

find_first_even([1, 3, 4, 5])
find_first_even([1, 3, 5])

found 4
no even number

That version also has a lurking bug: it reads n after the loop, which does not exist if numbers was empty. The for/else version has nowhere for that mistake to live.

while has the same clause, with the same meaning:

attempts = 0
while attempts < 3:
    attempts += 1
    if attempts == 5:
        break
else:
    print(f'gave up after {attempts} attempts')

gave up after 3 attempts

3.9 match

The match statement compares a value against a series of patterns, taking each case in turn, and — unlike a chain of ifs — it can destructure the value at the same time.

def http_status(code):
    match code:
        case 200:
            return 'OK'
        case 301 | 302:                       # alternatives
            return 'Redirect'
        case n if 400 <= n < 500:             # a guard
            return f'Client error ({n})'
        case n if n >= 500:
            return f'Server error ({n})'
        case _:                                # the wildcard: matches anything
            return f'Unknown ({code})'

for code in [200, 302, 404, 503, 100]:
    print(code, '->', http_status(code))

200 -> OK
302 -> Redirect
404 -> Client error (404)
503 -> Server error (503)
100 -> Unknown (100)

As a replacement for if/elif on plain values, that is a modest improvement. Its real power is structural matching — testing shape and extracting parts in one step:

def handle(event):
    match event:
        case {'type': 'click', 'pos': (x, y)}:
            return f'click at {x},{y}'
        case {'type': 'key', 'key': key, **rest}:
            return f'key {key!r} with {len(rest)} extra field(s)'
        case [first, *others]:
            return f'a list starting with {first!r} and {len(others)} more'
        case str() as text if text.startswith('cmd:'):
            return f'command {text[4:]!r}'
        case _:
            return 'unrecognised'

for e in [{'type': 'click', 'pos': (3, 4)},
          {'type': 'key', 'key': 'a', 'shift': True},
          [1, 2, 3],
          'cmd:save',
          42]:
    print(handle(e))

click at 3,4
key 'a' with 1 extra field(s)
a list starting with 1 and 2 more
command 'save'
unrecognised

Each case is doing three jobs at once: checking the type, checking the structure, and binding names to the parts. Written with if/isinstance/in/indexing, the first case alone is four lines and a try.

The patterns available:

Pattern Matches
case 200: that literal value
case 301 | 302: either alternative
case n: anything, binding it to n
case [a, b]: a sequence of exactly two, binding both
case [first, *rest]: a sequence of one or more
case {'k': v}: a mapping containing key k — extra keys are allowed
case Point(x=0, y=y): an instance with those attributes
case str() as s: an instance of a type, bound to s
case n if n > 0: with an extra condition
case _: anything, binding nothing

Two rules are essential and are where the mistakes are.

A bare name captures; it does not compare. This is the trap:

QUIT = 'quit'

def route(command):
    match command:
        case 'help':
            return 'helping'
        case QUIT:                   # captures ANYTHING into a local named QUIT
            return 'quitting'
    return f'unknown: {command}'

print(route('help'), '|', route('quit'), '|', route('xyzzy'))

helping | quitting | quitting

route('xyzzy') returned 'quitting'. case QUIT: did not compare against the constant — a bare, undotted name is a capture pattern, so it matched everything that reached it. Use a literal, or a dotted name, which does compare:

from enum import StrEnum

class Command(StrEnum):
    QUIT = 'quit'
    HELP = 'help'

def route(command):
    match command:
        case Command.HELP:           # dotted: compared, not captured
            return 'helping'
        case Command.QUIT:
            return 'quitting'
        case _:
            return f'unknown: {command}'

print(route('help'), '|', route('quit'), '|', route('xyzzy'))

helping | quitting | unknown: xyzzy

A mapping pattern matches a subset. case {'type': 'click'} matches a dictionary that has that key with that value, whatever else it contains — which is usually what you want for JSON, and is worth knowing so it does not surprise you. **rest captures the remainder if you need it.

When to use a match statement: dispatching on the shape of structured data — parsed JSON, an abstract syntax tree, an event, a command. When not to: a two-branch decision, or a lookup that a dictionary would do better (§4.10). match arrived in Python 3.10, so code that must run on older versions cannot use it.

Exercises

Exercise 3.1 — Predict eight. Say what each prints, then check.

print(bool(' '), bool(''), bool([0]), bool([]))
print(0 or 'a', 0 and 'a', '' or [], None or 0)
print(1 == True, 1 is True)
print([] == False)
Solution 
print(bool(' '), bool(''), bool([0]), bool([]))
print(0 or 'a', 0 and 'a', '' or [], None or 0)
print(1 == True, 1 is True)
print([] == False, bool([]) == False)

True False True False
a 0 [] 0
True False
False True

bool(' ') is True — a one-character string is not empty. bool([0]) is True — a one-item list is not empty, whatever the item is.

or and and return an operand, not a boolean. 0 or 'a' returns 'a' (the first truthy one); 0 and 'a' returns 0 (the first falsey one, short-circuiting so 'a' is never looked at); '' or [] returns [] because neither is truthy and or yields the last one; None or 0 returns 0 for the same reason.

1 == True is True but 1 is True is False. bool is a subclass of int with True == 1, so they compare equal — but they are different objects.

[] == False is False. This is the one people get wrong. An empty list is falsey, which is not the same as being equal to False. Equality between a list and a boolean is simply False, as it would be between a list and any other unrelated type. bool([]) == False is True, because that converts first.

The practical conclusion is the §3.4 rule: write if not items:, never if items == False: — the second is both longer and wrong.

Exercise 3.2 — Rewrite the pyramid. Rewrite this using guard clauses, and say what bug the rewrite makes visible.

def price_for(user, item):
    if user is not None:
        if user.get('active'):
            if item in user.get('cart', {}):
                if user.get('member'):
                    return item_price(item) * 0.9
                else:
                    return item_price(item)
            else:
                return None
        else:
            return None
    else:
        return None
Solution

Each else: return None is a guard turned inside out. Inverting the conditions and returning early flattens the whole thing:

PRICES = {'book': 10.0, 'pen': 2.0}

def item_price(item):
    return PRICES[item]

def price_for(user, item):
    if user is None:
        return None
    if not user.get('active'):
        return None
    if item not in user.get('cart', {}):
        return None
    price = item_price(item)
    return price * 0.9 if user.get('member') else price

cart = {'book': 1}
print(price_for(None, 'book'))
print(price_for({'active': False, 'cart': cart}, 'book'))
print(price_for({'active': True, 'cart': cart}, 'pen'))
print(price_for({'active': True, 'cart': cart}, 'book'))
print(price_for({'active': True, 'member': True, 'cart': cart}, 'book'))

None
None
None
10.0
9.0

Five levels of indentation became one, and the happy path is now the last two lines rather than buried in the middle.

The bug the rewrite makes visible: three different failures all return None. "No user", "suspended user" and "item not in cart" are entirely different situations, and the caller cannot tell them apart — it gets None and has to guess. Buried in the pyramid this was easy to miss; lined up as three consecutive guards it is obvious.

The better version says which:

PRICES = {'book': 10.0, 'pen': 2.0}

class PricingError(Exception):
    pass

def price_for(user, item):
    if user is None:
        raise PricingError('no user')
    if not user.get('active'):
        raise PricingError(f'user {user.get("id", "?")} is not active')
    if item not in user.get('cart', {}):
        raise PricingError(f'{item!r} is not in the cart')
    price = PRICES[item]
    return round(price * 0.9, 2) if user.get('member') else price

cart = {'book': 1}
for user in [None, {'active': False, 'id': 7}, {'active': True, 'cart': cart}]:
    try:
        print(price_for(user, 'pen'))
    except PricingError as e:
        print(f'PricingError: {e}')
print(price_for({'active': True, 'member': True, 'cart': cart}, 'book'))

PricingError: no user
PricingError: user 7 is not active
PricingError: 'pen' is not in the cart
9.0

Whether these should raise or return a result object is a design decision (§9.13). What is not a decision is that three distinct outcomes must be distinguishable — and flattening the nesting is what made that visible.

Exercise 3.3 — A match-based command parser. Write run(command) handling: ['quit']; ['add', item]; ['add', item, qty] where qty is a digit string; ['remove', item]; {'op': 'set', 'key': k, 'value': v}; and anything else as an error naming what was received.

Solution

The point of the exercise is that each case checks the shape and extracts the parts in one line — which is exactly what if/len/isinstance chains cannot do.

def run(command):
    match command:
        case ['quit'] | ['exit']:
            return 'quitting'
        case ['add', str(item), str(qty)] if qty.isdigit():
            return f'adding {int(qty)} x {item}'
        case ['add', str(item)]:
            return f'adding 1 x {item}'
        case ['add', *rest]:
            return f'add: expected 1 or 2 arguments, got {len(rest)}'
        case ['remove', str(item)]:
            return f'removing {item}'
        case {'op': 'set', 'key': key, 'value': value}:
            return f'set {key}={value!r}'
        case {'op': op}:
            return f'unknown op {op!r}'
        case []:
            return 'empty command'
        case _:
            return f'unrecognised: {command!r}'

for c in [['quit'], ['exit'],
          ['add', 'book'], ['add', 'book', '3'], ['add', 'book', 'many'],
          ['add', 'a', 'b', 'c'], ['remove', 'pen'],
          {'op': 'set', 'key': 'theme', 'value': 'dark'},
          {'op': 'reset'}, [], 42]:
    print(f'{str(c)[:34]:36} {run(c)}')

['quit']                             quitting
['exit']                             quitting
['add', 'book']                      adding 1 x book
['add', 'book', '3']                 adding 3 x book
['add', 'book', 'many']              add: expected 1 or 2 arguments, got 2
['add', 'a', 'b', 'c']               add: expected 1 or 2 arguments, got 3
['remove', 'pen']                    removing pen
{'op': 'set', 'key': 'theme', 'val   set theme='dark'
{'op': 'reset'}                      unknown op 'reset'
[]                                   empty command
42                                   unrecognised: 42

Four things the ordering is doing.

The most specific case comes first. ['add', str(item), str(qty)] if qty.isdigit() is tried before the two-element form and before the catch-all ['add', *rest]. Reverse them and the general case would swallow the specific ones — patterns are tried strictly top to bottom.

'many' falls through to the *rest case, producing a usage message rather than a crash. That is the guard failing, not the pattern: the shape matched, qty.isdigit() did not, so matching continued.

str(item) is a class pattern, not a call. It matches "an instance of str" and binds it to item. Without it, ['add', 3] would match ['add', str(item)]… it would not, in fact, and that is the point: the type check is part of the pattern, so a non-string item falls through to ['add', *rest].

The mapping cases are ordered general-last too. {'op': 'set', ...} requires three keys with op equal to 'set'; {'op': op} requires only that op exists and captures whatever it is. Note both would match a dictionary with additional keys, because mapping patterns match a subset.

The one thing to be careful about is case ['quit'] | ['exit']: — alternatives with | are fine as long as every alternative binds the same names, which here is none at all. case ['add', x] | ['remove', y]: would be a syntax error for exactly that reason.

SECTION 4

Functions

A function is a named piece of behaviour you can call. That much is true in every language. What makes Python's worth studying carefully is the argument system — six different kinds of parameter, each solving a real problem — and the scoping rules, which explain a family of bugs that are otherwise baffling. This section covers both, plus lambdas, docstrings, annotations, closures and recursion.

4.1 Defining and Calling

def greet(name):
    """Return a greeting for name."""
    return f'Hello, {name}!'

print(greet('Ada'))
print(greet(name='Grace'))
print(greet.__doc__)
print(type(greet).__name__)

Hello, Ada!
Hello, Grace!
Return a greeting for name.
function

def binds a name to a function object. That object is an ordinary value — it can be stored in a list, passed to another function, or returned from one (§4.10).

A function with no return statement returns None. So does a bare return:

def shout(text):
    print(text.upper())

def early(x):
    if x < 0:
        return
    return x * 2

result = shout('hello')
print(result)
print(early(5), early(-5))

HELLO
None
10 None

That is the mechanism behind x = mylist.sort() giving None (§6.2), and behind the mystifying TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable that follows using the result of a function that only printed.

A return statement can hand back several values, which is really one tuple (§6.5):

def divide(a, b):
    return a // b, a % b

quotient, remainder = divide(17, 5)
print(quotient, remainder)
print(divide(17, 5))
print(type(divide(17, 5)).__name__)

3 2
(3, 2)
tuple

4.2 Positional and Keyword Arguments

Arguments can be passed by position or by name:

def rect(width, height, unit='px'):
    return f'{width}x{height}{unit}'

print(rect(3, 4))
print(rect(3, 4, 'em'))
print(rect(width=3, height=4))
print(rect(height=4, width=3))          # keyword order does not matter
print(rect(3, unit='em', height=4))     # positional first, then keywords

3x4px
3x4em
3x4px
3x4px
3x4em

Positional arguments must come before keyword ones, and a name cannot be supplied twice:

def rect(width, height):
    return f'{width}x{height}'

try:
    eval("rect(width=3, 4)")
except SyntaxError as e:
    print(f'SyntaxError: {e.msg}')
try:
    rect(3, width=4)
except TypeError as e:
    print(f'TypeError: {e}')
try:
    rect(3)
except TypeError as e:
    print(f'TypeError: {e}')

SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument
TypeError: rect() got multiple values for argument 'width'
TypeError: rect() missing 1 required positional argument: 'height'

Use keyword arguments at the call site whenever the meaning is not obvious. send(msg, True, False) tells a reader nothing; send(msg, urgent=True, retry=False) tells them everything, and survives someone reordering the parameters.

4.3 Default Arguments, and the Mutable Default Trap

A default makes a parameter optional:

def connect(host, port=5432, timeout=30, ssl=True):
    return f'{host}:{port} timeout={timeout} ssl={ssl}'

print(connect('db.example.com'))
print(connect('db.example.com', 5433))
print(connect('db.example.com', ssl=False))

db.example.com:5432 timeout=30 ssl=True
db.example.com:5433 timeout=30 ssl=True
db.example.com:5432 timeout=30 ssl=False

Parameters with defaults must come after those without, for the obvious reason that otherwise there would be no way to supply the later one positionally.

Now the trap, and it is the most famous one in Python. A default value is evaluated once, when the def statement runs — not on each call.

def add(item, target=[]):
    target.append(item)
    return target

print(add('a'))
print(add('b'))
print(add('c'))
print(add.__defaults__)

['a']
