print(cities)

['London', 'Paris', 'Tokyo']

The four reading methods, and when each is right:

for line in f — the default. Lazy, holds one line at a time, works on a file of any size.
f.read() — the whole file as one string. Fine when you know it is small, or when you need to search across lines.
f.readlines() — a list of every line. Loads everything; only use it when you genuinely need a list.
f.readline() — one line. Rarely needed; useful for reading a header before looping over the rest.

Writing has two: write takes a string and adds no newline of its own, and writelines takes an iterable of strings and also adds nothing.

import tempfile, os

path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), 'out.txt')
rows = ['alpha', 'beta', 'gamma']

with open(path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.writelines(line + '\n' for line in rows)     # newlines are YOUR job
    print('a', 'b', sep='|', file=f)               # print() works on files too

with open(path, encoding='utf-8') as f:
    print(repr(f.read()))

'alpha\nbeta\ngamma\na|b\n'

print(..., file=f) is often the most convenient writer: it handles the newline, the separator and the conversion to string.

10.4 pathlib: Paths as Objects

Building paths by joining strings works until it does not — a missing separator, a doubled one, a Windows backslash. pathlib.Path treats a path as a structured object with methods.

from pathlib import Path

p = Path('/home/ada/reports/q3.csv')
print(p.name, p.stem, p.suffix)
print(p.parent)
print(p.parts)
print(p.with_suffix('.json'))
print(p.parent / 'q4.csv')                 # / joins paths
print(Path('data') / 'raw' / 'file.csv')

q3.csv q3 .csv
/home/ada/reports
('/', 'home', 'ada', 'reports', 'q3.csv')
/home/ada/reports/q3.json
/home/ada/reports/q4.csv
data/raw/file.csv

The / operator is the headline feature and it is genuinely better than os.path.join: it reads like a path, it inserts the correct separator for the platform, and it works with strings on either side.

Asking questions about a path, and the read/write shortcuts:

from pathlib import Path
import tempfile

base = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
f = base / 'notes.txt'

print(f.exists(), f.is_file())
f.write_text('hello from pathlib\n', encoding='utf-8')
print(f.exists(), f.is_file(), f.is_dir())
print(repr(f.read_text(encoding='utf-8')))
print(f.stat().st_size, 'bytes')

(base / 'sub' / 'deeper').mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
print((base / 'sub' / 'deeper').is_dir())

f.unlink()
print('after unlink:', f.exists())

False False
True True False
'hello from pathlib\n'
19 bytes
True
after unlink: False

write_text and read_text open, do the operation and close, in one call — perfect for small files and the reason a great deal of with open(...) boilerplate is unnecessary. mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) creates intermediate directories and does not complain if the directory is already there, which is what you almost always want.

Listing directory contents, and glob patterns for matching by name:

from pathlib import Path
import tempfile

base = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
for name in ['a.txt', 'b.txt', 'c.csv']:
    (base / name).write_text('x', encoding='utf-8')
(base / 'sub').mkdir()
(base / 'sub' / 'd.txt').write_text('y', encoding='utf-8')

print(sorted(p.name for p in base.iterdir()))
print(sorted(p.name for p in base.glob('*.txt')))
print(sorted(str(p.relative_to(base)) for p in base.rglob('*.txt')))
print(sorted(p.name for p in base.glob('[ab].*')))

['a.txt', 'b.txt', 'c.csv', 'sub']
['a.txt', 'b.txt']
['a.txt', 'b.txt', 'sub/d.txt']
['a.txt', 'b.txt']

iterdir() lists one level. glob(pattern) matches within one level, where * matches any run of characters, ? matches one, and [abc] matches one of a set. rglob(pattern) — equivalently glob('**/pattern') — searches recursively, which is how you find every .py file in a project in one line.

Three more paths worth knowing:

from pathlib import Path

print(Path.home().is_absolute())
print(Path.cwd().is_absolute())
print(Path('a/../b/./c.txt').as_posix())
print(str(Path('~/notes.txt').expanduser()).startswith('/'))

True
True
a/../b/c.txt
True

Note that Path removed the redundant . but kept the ... That is deliberate: a/../b is only the same as b when a is a real directory and not a symbolic link, so resolving it is a question for the filesystem rather than for string manipulation. resolve() asks the filesystem and gives you the real answer.

10.5 Encodings, and Why to Always Say utf-8

A file on disk holds bytes. Text is a decoding of those bytes, and the mapping is the encoding. Get it wrong and you get either mojibake or an exception.

text = 'café — naïve 日本'

utf8 = text.encode('utf-8')
latin1 = text.encode('latin-1', errors='replace')
print(len(text), 'characters')
print(len(utf8), 'bytes as utf-8')
print(utf8[:8])
print(latin1.decode('latin-1'))

15 characters
23 bytes as utf-8
b'caf\xc3\xa9 \xe2\x80'
café ? naïve ??

UTF-8 uses one byte for ASCII characters and two to four for everything else, which is why 15 characters became 23 bytes. Latin-1 has 256 slots. It covers é and ï, so those survived; it has no room for the em dash or the Japanese characters, and errors='replace' turned each of those into a ? — permanently, because the original character is not recoverable from a question mark.

Decoding with the wrong encoding is worse, because it often succeeds:

text = 'café'
raw = text.encode('utf-8')

print(raw)
print(raw.decode('utf-8'))
print(raw.decode('latin-1'))            # succeeds, and is wrong
try:
    raw.decode('ascii')
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    print(f'UnicodeDecodeError: {e.reason}')

b'caf\xc3\xa9'
café
cafÃ©
UnicodeDecodeError: ordinal not in range(128)

cafÃ© is the classic symptom — bytes written as UTF-8 and read as Latin-1. Nothing raised; the data is simply corrupt from here on.

Always pass encoding='utf-8' explicitly when opening a text file. Without it, Python uses a platform default that differs between machines, so a file that reads correctly on your Linux laptop can raise on a colleague's Windows machine and produce mojibake on a third. That one keyword removes an entire category of "works on my machine".

For files that are not text at all — images, archives, anything binary — use binary mode and work with bytes:

import tempfile, os

path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), 'blob.bin')

with open(path, 'wb') as f:
    f.write(bytes([0x89, 0x50, 0x4E, 0x47, 0x0D, 0x0A, 0x1A, 0x0A]))

with open(path, 'rb') as f:
    header = f.read(8)

print(header)
print(header.hex())
print(header[:4] == b'\x89PNG')

b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n'
89504e470d0a1a0a
True

In binary mode there is no encoding and no newline translation: what you write is exactly what lands on disk. Never open a binary file in text mode — the decode will either fail or silently mangle it.

10.6 JSON

JSON is the standard format for exchanging structured data. Python's json module converts between JSON text and Python objects.

import json

data = {
    'name': 'Ada',
    'age': 36,
    'languages': ['python', 'assembly'],
    'active': True,
    'manager': None,
    'score': 9.5,
}

text = json.dumps(data)
print(text)
print(json.dumps(data, indent=2, sort_keys=True)[:60])

back = json.loads(text)
print(back == data, type(back).__name__)

{"name": "Ada", "age": 36, "languages": ["python", "assembly"], "active": true, "manager": null, "score": 9.5}
{
  "active": true,
  "age": 36,
  "languages": [
    "pytho
True dict

Four functions, and the naming is worth learning properly because it trips people up: dumps/loads work with strings (the s is for string), dump/load work with file objects.

import json, tempfile, os
from pathlib import Path

path = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / 'config.json'
config = {'host': 'example.com', 'port': 8443, 'debug': False}

with open(path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    json.dump(config, f, indent=2)

with open(path, encoding='utf-8') as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)

print(loaded)
print(path.read_text(encoding='utf-8'))

{'host': 'example.com', 'port': 8443, 'debug': False}
{
  "host": "example.com",
  "port": 8443,
  "debug": false
}

The type mapping is not one-to-one, and the asymmetries cause real bugs:

Python JSON Coming back
dict object dict
list, tuple array list — a tuple becomes a list
str string str
int, float number int or float
True / False true / false bool
None null None
set, datetime, custom class — TypeError 
import json

original = {'tags': ('a', 'b'), 'when': 3}
back = json.loads(json.dumps(original))
print(back)
print(type(back['tags']).__name__)

try:
    json.dumps({'tags': {'a', 'b'}})
except TypeError as e:
    print(f'TypeError: {e}')

{'tags': ['a', 'b'], 'when': 3}
list
TypeError: Object of type set is not JSON serializable

A tuple round-trips into a list, silently. And a set, a datetime or an object of your own raises. The fix is a default function that converts anything unknown into something JSON can hold:

import json
from datetime import date, datetime

def to_json(value):
    if isinstance(value, (date, datetime)):
        return value.isoformat()
    if isinstance(value, set):
        return sorted(value)
    raise TypeError(f'cannot serialise {type(value).__name__}')

data = {'created': date(2026, 8, 24), 'tags': {'b', 'a'}}
print(json.dumps(data, default=to_json))

{"created": "2026-08-24", "tags": ["a", "b"]}

Note also that JSON object keys are always strings. A dict with integer keys survives dumps by having them converted, and comes back with string keys — another silent asymmetry:

import json

print(json.loads(json.dumps({1: 'a', 2: 'b'})))

{'1': 'a', '2': 'b'}

And malformed input raises a JSONDecodeError (a subclass of ValueError) that tells you where:

import json

try:
    json.loads('{"a": 1, "b": }')
except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
    print(f'{type(e).__name__} at line {e.lineno} column {e.colno}: {e.msg}')

JSONDecodeError at line 1 column 15: Expecting value

10.7 CSV

CSV is the format spreadsheets and databases export. It looks trivial — commas between values — and is not: values can contain commas, quotes and newlines, and handling that correctly is exactly what the csv module is for.

import csv, io

rows = [
    ['name', 'city', 'note'],
    ['Ada', 'London', 'likes commas, apparently'],
    ['Grace', 'New York', 'said "hello"'],
    ['Alan', 'Wilmslow', 'two\nlines'],
]

buf = io.StringIO()
writer = csv.writer(buf)
writer.writerows(rows)
print(buf.getvalue())

name,city,note
Ada,London,"likes commas, apparently"
Grace,New York,"said ""hello"""
Alan,Wilmslow,"two
lines"

Look at what the module did unprompted: quoted the value containing a comma, doubled the internal quotes, and quoted the value containing a newline. This is why you never split a CSV line on commas yourself — the naive version breaks on the second row and mangles the third and fourth.

Reading it back gives the original data exactly:

import csv, io

text = ('name,city,note\r\n'
        'Ada,London,"likes commas, apparently"\r\n'
        'Grace,New York,"said ""hello"""\r\n')

for row in csv.reader(io.StringIO(text)):
    print(row)

['name', 'city', 'note']
['Ada', 'London', 'likes commas, apparently']
['Grace', 'New York', 'said "hello"']

DictReader and DictWriter use the header row as keys, which makes the code readable and immune to column reordering:

import csv, io

text = 'name,age,city\nAda,36,London\nGrace,45,New York\n'

reader = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text))
people = list(reader)
print(people[0])
print([p['name'] for p in people])
print(sum(int(p['age']) for p in people))

{'name': 'Ada', 'age': '36', 'city': 'London'}
['Ada', 'Grace']
81

Every value read from a CSV is a string. There are no types in the format, so '36' is what you get and converting is your job — that int(p['age']) is not optional.

Writing with DictWriter:

import csv, io

people = [{'name': 'Ada', 'age': 36}, {'name': 'Grace', 'age': 45}]

buf = io.StringIO()
writer = csv.DictWriter(buf, fieldnames=['name', 'age'])
writer.writeheader()
writer.writerows(people)
print(repr(buf.getvalue()))

'name,age\r\nAda,36\r\nGrace,45\r\n'

Two details for real files. Open a CSV file with newline='' — the module handles line endings itself, and without that argument Python's newline translation can produce blank lines between rows on some platforms. And CSV files in the wild are frequently not comma-separated; csv.reader(f, delimiter='\t') handles TSV, and csv.Sniffer can guess.

import csv, io, tempfile, os

path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), 'people.csv')

with open(path, 'w', newline='', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=['name', 'age'])
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerow({'name': 'Ada', 'age': 36})

with open(path, newline='', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    print(list(csv.DictReader(f)))

[{'name': 'Ada', 'age': '36'}]

10.8 Choosing a Format, and Failing Safely

JSON — nested structures, APIs, configuration, anything a program wrote for another program. Types survive (mostly). Not for very large data: it must be parsed whole.
CSV — flat rows, spreadsheets, exports, anything a human might open. No types, no nesting, streams one row at a time so size is not a problem.
Plain text — logs, notes, anything append-only and line-oriented.
SQLite — in the standard library as sqlite3. Once you want to query, index or update rows rather than rewrite the whole file, a database is the answer and a file format is not.

Finally, the failure modes. File operations fail for reasons entirely outside your program, and the exceptions are worth handling by name (§9.3):

import tempfile, os
from pathlib import Path

base = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())

for path in [base / 'nope.txt', base, base / 'ok.txt']:
    (base / 'ok.txt').write_text('fine', encoding='utf-8')
    try:
        print(f'{path.name[:4]}: read {len(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))} chars')
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print('nope.txt: not found')
    except IsADirectoryError:
        print('the base dir: that is a directory')
    except PermissionError:
        print('no permission')

nope.txt: not found
the base dir: that is a directory
ok.t: read 4 chars

Three different outcomes from the same three lines of handling. All of those exceptions inherit from OSError (§9.3), so except OSError catches the lot when you do not need to distinguish them — and e.strerror then gives the operating system's own message for whichever it was.

One structural warning: do not check-then-open.

from pathlib import Path
import tempfile

p = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / 'x.txt'

if p.exists():                       # racy: the file can vanish right here
    text = p.read_text(encoding='utf-8')
else:
    text = 'default'
print(repr(text))

try:                                 # better: just try it
    text = p.read_text(encoding='utf-8')
except FileNotFoundError:
    text = 'default'
print(repr(text))

'default'
'default'

Between the exists() and the read_text() another process can delete the file, and your "safe" code raises anyway. Attempting the operation and handling the failure has no such gap — and it is one fewer filesystem call.

Exercises

Exercise 10.1 — Find and fix five faults. This function is meant to load a config file and fall back to defaults. It has five distinct problems.

import json

def load_config(path):
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        return {}
    f = open(path)
    data = json.loads(f.read())
    config = {}
    for line in data:
        config[line] = data[line]
    return config
Solution

1. os is used but never imported. A NameError on the first call, and the kind of thing a linter (§14.8) reports instantly.

2. open(path) has no encoding. The platform default is used, so the same file reads differently on different machines (§10.5).

3. The file is never closed. No with, no close() — the handle leaks, and on a function called in a loop the process eventually runs out of them (§10.2).

4. exists() then open() is a race (§10.8), and it is also redundant: the open would raise FileNotFoundError anyway, which is what you would handle.

5. The whole loop is an inefficient copy. for line in data: config[line] = data[line] is dict(data), written out — and the variable name line says the author thought they were iterating over lines of a file rather than keys of a dict.

There is a sixth, arguably worse than any of them: a malformed file raises JSONDecodeError and the caller has no idea why, since the function's contract implies it either loads the config or falls back.

The rewrite:

import json
from pathlib import Path

DEFAULTS = {'host': 'localhost', 'port': 8080, 'debug': False}

def load_config(path):
    """Return DEFAULTS updated with whatever the file contains."""
    try:
        text = Path(path).read_text(encoding='utf-8')
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return dict(DEFAULTS)
    try:
        data = json.loads(text)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        raise ValueError(f'{path}: line {e.lineno} column {e.colno}: {e.msg}') from e
    if not isinstance(data, dict):
        raise ValueError(f'{path}: expected a JSON object, got {type(data).__name__}')
    return {**DEFAULTS, **data}

import tempfile
base = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())

print(load_config(base / 'missing.json'))

(base / 'good.json').write_text('{"port": 9000}', encoding='utf-8')
print(load_config(base / 'good.json'))

(base / 'bad.json').write_text('{"port": }', encoding='utf-8')
try:
    load_config(base / 'bad.json')
except ValueError as e:
    print('ValueError:', str(e).split('/')[-1])

(base / 'list.json').write_text('[1, 2]', encoding='utf-8')
try:
    load_config(base / 'list.json')
except ValueError as e:
    print('ValueError:', str(e).split('/')[-1])

{'host': 'localhost', 'port': 8080, 'debug': False}
{'host': 'localhost', 'port': 9000, 'debug': False}
ValueError: bad.json: line 1 column 10: Expecting value
ValueError: list.json: expected a JSON object, got list

Beyond the five fixes: a missing file is a normal condition and returns defaults, while a malformed file is an error and raises with the line and column — the §9.13 distinction between the exceptional and the expected. {**DEFAULTS, **data} merges so that a partial config only overrides what it mentions. And dict(DEFAULTS) copies, so a caller mutating the result cannot corrupt the module-level defaults for everyone else (§11.4's shared-mutable trap, in a different costume).

Exercise 10.2 — CSV to JSON, correctly. Write csv_to_json(csv_text) that converts CSV text to a JSON array of objects, converting any column that is entirely integers to integers and any column that is entirely true/false to booleans. Leave everything else as strings.

Solution

The subtlety is "entirely" — you cannot decide a column's type from its first value, because a column of 1, 2, unknown is text. So the rows must be read fully, then each column examined as a whole.

import csv, io, json

def _convert_column(values):
    """Return (converted_values) with a type inferred from ALL the values."""
    if values and all(v.strip().lstrip('-').isdigit() for v in values):
        return [int(v) for v in values]
    if values and all(v.strip().lower() in ('true', 'false') for v in values):
        return [v.strip().lower() == 'true' for v in values]
    return values

def csv_to_json(csv_text, indent=None):
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_text)))
    if not rows:
        return json.dumps([])
    columns = {name: _convert_column([r[name] for r in rows]) for name in rows[0]}
    records = [{name: columns[name][i] for name in columns} for i in range(len(rows))]
    return json.dumps(records, indent=indent)

text = ('name,age,active,note\n'
        'Ada,36,true,"likes commas, apparently"\n'
        'Grace,45,false,said hello\n')
print(csv_to_json(text))
print()
print(csv_to_json('name,age\nAda,unknown\nGrace,45\n'))
print(csv_to_json('name,age\n'))

[{"name": "Ada", "age": 36, "active": true, "note": "likes commas, apparently"}, {"name": "Grace", "age": 45, "active": false, "note": "said hello"}]

[{"name": "Ada", "age": "unknown"}, {"name": "Grace", "age": "45"}]
[]

Three things the tests above are checking.

The quoted field with a comma survived, because csv.DictReader parsed it rather than a split(',') — the §10.7 point, now load-bearing.

The mixed column stayed as strings. age in the second call has one non-numeric value, so 45 remains "45" rather than becoming an int while its neighbour stays text. A column with inconsistent types is a data problem, and quietly converting half of it would hide that.

A header-only file gives [], not a crash. Empty input is the boundary that breaks naive implementations, and if not rows is the whole fix.

Note v.strip().lstrip('-').isdigit() rather than a try: int(v). Either works; isdigit was chosen so that '1.5' stays a string — floats were not part of the specification, and silently turning '1.50' into 1.5 would lose the trailing zero that a price column needs.

Exercise 10.3 — A safe atomic write. Write save_json(path, data) that writes JSON to a file such that a crash mid-write cannot leave a truncated or corrupt file behind. The previous contents must survive intact if anything goes wrong.

Solution

open(path, 'w') truncates the file immediately, before a single byte is written, so a crash at any point after that leaves a broken file and no way back. The standard answer is write to a temporary file in the same directory, then rename it over the target — because a rename within one filesystem is atomic: it either happened or it did not, and no reader ever sees a half-written file.

import json, os, tempfile
from pathlib import Path

def save_json(path, data, indent=2):
    path = Path(path)
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, prefix=path.name + '.', suffix='.tmp')
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
            json.dump(data, f, indent=indent)
            f.flush()
            os.fsync(f.fileno())          # force it to the disk, not just the OS buffer
        os.replace(tmp, path)             # atomic within one filesystem
    except BaseException:
        Path(tmp).unlink(missing_ok=True)
        raise

base = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
target = base / 'config.json'

save_json(target, {'port': 8080})
print(target.read_text(encoding='utf-8'))

class Unserialisable:
    pass

try:
    save_json(target, {'port': 9000, 'bad': Unserialisable()})
except TypeError as e:
    print('TypeError:', str(e).split(' is not')[0])

print('previous contents intact:', json.loads(target.read_text(encoding='utf-8')))
print('no leftover temp files:', [p.name for p in base.iterdir()])

{
  "port": 8080
}
TypeError: Object of type Unserialisable
previous contents intact: {'port': 8080}
no leftover temp files: ['config.json']

The second save_json failed half way through serialising — json.dump writes incrementally, so {"port": 9000, "bad": had already gone into the temporary file when the TypeError was raised. With a plain open(path, 'w') that fragment would now be the entire contents of config.json. Here the original is untouched, because the rename never happened.

Four details each doing a specific job:

dir=path.parent puts the temporary file on the same filesystem as the target. os.replace across filesystems is not atomic — it degrades to a copy — so a temp file in /tmp would silently lose the guarantee.

os.replace, not os.rename. They are the same on Linux, but os.rename fails on Windows if the destination exists, and os.replace is defined to overwrite everywhere.

f.flush() and os.fsync() push the data out of Python's buffer and then out of the operating system's, so that a power failure immediately after the rename cannot leave a renamed-but-empty file. Without them the rename can reach the disk before the contents do.

except BaseException — deliberately broader than the except Exception §9.13 recommends. This is one of the rare justified cases: the temporary file must be cleaned up even on KeyboardInterrupt or SystemExit, and the bare raise immediately re-raises, so nothing is swallowed. The try/finally form would be equally correct.

This pattern is worth keeping. Any time a program overwrites a file it will need again, "write elsewhere, then rename" is the difference between a crash costing nothing and a crash costing the file.

SECTION 11

Classes and Objects

Every value you have used so far is an object: an integer, a list, a file, a function. A class is how you make a new kind of object — one that bundles data with the operations that belong to it, and that Python's own machinery (len, in, for, print, +) will cooperate with once you tell it how. This section takes you from the syntax to the point where you can read the class definitions in someone else's codebase without guessing.

11.1 Why Classes Exist

Before the syntax, the motivation — because classes are frequently taught as "the next feature" and then used where a function would have been better.

Here is a program written without classes. It tracks bank accounts as dictionaries:

def make_account(owner, balance=0):
    return {'owner': owner, 'balance': balance}

def deposit(account, amount):
    account['balance'] += amount

def withdraw(account, amount):
    if amount > account['balance']:
        raise ValueError('insufficient funds')
    account['balance'] -= amount

acct = make_account('Ada', 100)
deposit(acct, 50)
withdraw(acct, 30)
print(acct)

{'owner': 'Ada', 'balance': 120}

This works. It is also fragile in three specific ways, and each one is a thing classes fix.

Nothing enforces the shape. account['balence'] = 5 silently adds a fourth key. Nothing says an account has an owner and a balance; that knowledge lives only in the heads of the people who wrote deposit and withdraw.

The data and the operations are not connected. withdraw is a plain function that happens to expect an account-shaped dictionary. Pass it a dictionary describing a user and it fails somewhere in the middle, half-done. Nothing links the three functions to the one kind of data they belong to.

There is no way to guard the invariant. The rule "balance is never negative" is enforced inside withdraw and nowhere else, so acct['balance'] = -900 is one keystroke away and the program has no way to notice.

A class is Python's answer to all three: a named type whose instances carry known attributes, whose operations are reached through the object, and whose internals you can put a gate in front of.

class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError('insufficient funds')
        self.balance -= amount

acct = Account('Ada', 100)
acct.deposit(50)
acct.withdraw(30)
print(acct.owner, acct.balance)

Ada 120

When not to reach for a class. If a thing has no state that outlives a single call, it is a function. A class with one method and no attributes is a function wearing a costume; a class whose __init__ stores three values that are then only read is often better as a dataclass (§11.10) or a plain tuple. The test is: is there state, and are there several operations that must agree about it? Two yeses mean a class.

11.2 Defining a Class, and What self Is

The syntax is class followed by a name — CapWords by convention, always — and an indented body:

class Dog:
    """A dog, for demonstration purposes."""

    def bark(self):
        return 'Woof'

d = Dog()
print(type(d))
print(d.bark())
print(Dog.__doc__)

<class '__main__.Dog'>
Woof
A dog, for demonstration purposes.

Two things happened in d = Dog(). Python created a new empty object of type Dog, and — because Dog defines no __init__ — handed it straight back. The docstring (§4.11) written first in the body became Dog.__doc__, exactly as a function's does.

self is not a keyword. It is an ordinary parameter that receives the instance, and it is the first parameter of every method by convention so strongly held that violating it will confuse every reader you have. The mechanism is worth seeing directly:

class Dog:
    def bark(self):
        return f'{self} says Woof'

d = Dog()
print(Dog.bark(d))          # the plain function, called with the instance explicitly
print(d.bark())             # the same call, with d supplied automatically

<__main__.Dog object at 0x0> says Woof
<__main__.Dog object at 0x0> says Woof

d.bark() and Dog.bark(d) are the same call. Looking up a function attribute on an instance produces a bound method — the function with its first argument already filled in — and calling it passes the instance through. That is the whole of it, and it explains the error message every beginner meets:

class Dog:
    def bark():
        return 'Woof'

try:
    Dog().bark()
except TypeError as e:
    print(e)

Dog.bark() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given

The "1 was given" is the instance. Nothing exotic is happening; you wrote a function taking nothing and Python called it with one argument.

11.3 __init__ and Instance Variables

__init__ runs immediately after the object is created and is where instance state is set up. It is not a constructor in the C++ or Java sense — the object already exists when it runs — but it fills the same role in practice.

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def distance_from_origin(self):
        return (self.x ** 2 + self.y ** 2) ** 0.5

p = Point(3, 4)
print(p.x, p.y)
print(p.distance_from_origin())
print(p.__dict__)

3 4
5.0
{'x': 3, 'y': 4}

An instance variable is any attribute assigned through self. They live in the instance's own __dict__, which is a real dictionary you can inspect — that printout is the whole of p's state. Nothing pre-declares x and y; the assignment in __init__ creates them.

Because the assignment creates them, an attribute set only inside an if exists only sometimes, which is a genuinely common bug:

class Config:
    def __init__(self, debug=False):
        if debug:
            self.log_level = 'DEBUG'

c = Config()
try:
    print(c.log_level)
except AttributeError as e:
    print(e)

'Config' object has no attribute 'log_level'

The fix is to always assign, in every branch: set self.log_level = 'DEBUG' if debug else 'INFO'. Give every attribute a value in __init__ unconditionally, and readers of your class can trust that the attributes they see there are the attributes it has.

11.4 Class Variables, and the Trap in Them

An assignment in the class body — not through self — makes a class variable: one object, shared by every instance and by the class itself.

class Dog:
    species = 'Canis familiaris'      # class variable: one, shared

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name             # instance variable: one per dog

a, b = Dog('Rex'), Dog('Fido')
print(a.species, b.species, Dog.species)
print(a.name, b.name)

Canis familiaris Canis familiaris Canis familiaris
Rex Fido

Attribute lookup checks the instance first, then the class. So a class variable acts as a default that any instance can override — and the override goes into the instance, leaving the class variable untouched:

class Dog:
    species = 'Canis familiaris'

a, b = Dog(), Dog()
a.species = 'Canis lupus'            # creates an *instance* variable on a
print(a.species, b.species, Dog.species)
print(a.__dict__, b.__dict__)

Canis lupus Canis familiaris Canis familiaris
{'species': 'Canis lupus'} {}

Now the trap. That "the assignment goes into the instance" rule only applies to assignment. A mutation has no assignment in it, so it reaches straight through to the shared object:

class Dog:
    tricks = []                       # WRONG: one list, shared by every dog

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def learn(self, trick):
        self.tricks.append(trick)     # mutates the class variable

a, b = Dog('Rex'), Dog('Fido')
a.learn('roll over')
b.learn('play dead')
print(a.tricks)
print(b.tricks)
print(a.tricks is b.tricks)

['roll over', 'play dead']
['roll over', 'play dead']
True

Rex knows a trick nobody taught him. This is the same mechanism as the mutable-default-argument trap in §4.3, and it has the same fix: mutable state belongs in __init__.

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.tricks = []              # a fresh list per dog

a, b = Dog('Rex'), Dog('Fido')
a.tricks.append('roll over')
b.tricks.append('play dead')
print(a.tricks, b.tricks)

['roll over'] ['play dead']

The rule that avoids the whole family of bugs: class variables should be immutable — a string, a number, a tuple, a constant. If it can be mutated, put it in __init__.

11.5 Three Kinds of Method

Most methods take self. Two decorators (§4.13 introduced the syntax; here is the first place you will really use them) produce the other two kinds.

class Temperature:
    absolute_zero_c = -273.15                 # class variable

    def __init__(self, celsius):
        self.celsius = celsius

    def to_fahrenheit(self):                  # instance method: needs this reading
        return self.celsius * 9 / 5 + 32

    @classmethod
    def from_fahrenheit(cls, f):              # class method: needs the class
        return cls((f - 32) * 5 / 9)

    @staticmethod
    def is_valid(celsius):                    # static method: needs neither
        return celsius >= Temperature.absolute_zero_c

t = Temperature(100)
print(t.to_fahrenheit())
print(Temperature.from_fahrenheit(212).celsius)
print(Temperature.is_valid(-300), Temperature.is_valid(20))

212.0
100.0
False True

An instance method takes self and works on one object's data. A class method takes cls — the class itself — and its overwhelmingly common use is exactly the one above: an alternative constructor. Writing cls(...) rather than Temperature(...) matters the moment anyone subclasses you, because cls is the actual class that was called:

class Temperature:
    def __init__(self, celsius):
        self.celsius = celsius

    @classmethod
    def from_fahrenheit(cls, f):
        return cls((f - 32) * 5 / 9)

class OvenTemperature(Temperature):
    pass

t = OvenTemperature.from_fahrenheit(350)
print(type(t).__name__, round(t.celsius, 1))

OvenTemperature 176.7

Had from_fahrenheit hard-coded Temperature(...), that would print Temperature and the subclass would be silently useless.

A static method is a plain function that lives in the class's namespace because that is where it belongs conceptually. It gets no automatic first argument. If you find yourself writing many of them, ask whether they want to be module-level functions instead — often they do.

11.6 Inheritance

A class can be defined in terms of another, taking everything it has and changing what needs changing. The base class goes in parentheses:

class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def speak(self):
        return '...'

    def describe(self):
        return f'{self.name} says {self.speak()}'

class Dog(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return 'Woof'

class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return 'Meow'

for a in [Animal('Thing'), Dog('Rex'), Cat('Tom')]:
    print(a.describe())

Thing says ...
Rex says Woof
Tom says Meow

Dog never defines __init__ or describe; it inherits both. And notice what describe does: it calls self.speak(), and self is a Dog, so Dog.speak runs. A method defined in the base class calls the most derived override. That is polymorphism, and it is inheritance's actual point — not code reuse, which a function would also give you, but the ability to write describe once against a method whose implementation is chosen per object.

Two built-ins ask about the relationship:

class Animal: pass
class Dog(Animal): pass

d = Dog()
print(isinstance(d, Dog), isinstance(d, Animal), isinstance(d, str))
print(issubclass(Dog, Animal), issubclass(Animal, Dog))
print(Dog.__bases__, Dog.__mro__)

True True False
True False
(<class '__main__.Animal'>,) (<class '__main__.Dog'>, <class '__main__.Animal'>, <class 'object'>)

isinstance asks about an object, issubclass about a class, and both are true "or a subclass of" — a Dog genuinely is an Animal. Note object at the end of that last tuple: every class in Python inherits from object, whether you say so or not.

11.7 super() and Extending Rather Than Replacing

Overriding replaces the base method entirely. Usually you want to add to it, and super() is how you call the version you are overriding:

class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        super().__init__(name)        # let Animal set up name
        self.breed = breed

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Dog({self.name!r}, {self.breed!r})'

print(Dog('Rex', 'collie'))

Dog('Rex', 'collie')

Forgetting the super().__init__(...) call is the single most common inheritance bug, and it fails later rather than immediately: the object is built fine and then something reads self.name and gets an AttributeError from a completely different part of the program.

Write super() with no arguments. The older Animal.__init__(self, name) spelling still works and is what you will see in code written before Python 3, but it names the base class twice — in the class line and again in the call — so renaming the base leaves a lie behind. It also gets multiple inheritance wrong, which is the subject of §11.9.

11.8 Special Methods: Making Your Object Behave Like a Built-in

Names of the form __name__ are dunder (double-underscore) methods, also called special methods or magic methods. You almost never call them directly; Python calls them for you when a piece of syntax or a built-in function is applied to your object. Implementing them is how a class of yours becomes as convenient to use as a list.

Start with the two that print:

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Point({self.x}, {self.y})'      # for developers

    def __str__(self):
        return f'({self.x}, {self.y})'           # for users

p = Point(1, 2)
print(p)              # uses __str__
print(repr(p))        # uses __repr__
print([p])            # a container always uses __repr__ of its items

(1, 2)
Point(1, 2)
[Point(1, 2)]

Always write __repr__. Without it you get <__main__.Point object at 0x7f...> in every debugging session, every log line and every list printout. __str__ is optional and falls back to __repr__. The convention for __repr__ is that it should look like the code that would recreate the object — which is why the Dog example above used !r on the strings, so they print with quotes.

Equality and hashing come next, and they come as a pair:

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Point({self.x}, {self.y})'

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Point):
            return NotImplemented
        return (self.x, self.y) == (other.x, other.y)

    def __hash__(self):
        return hash((self.x, self.y))

a, b = Point(1, 2), Point(1, 2)
print(a == b, a is b)
print({a, b})                       # equal and same hash: one entry
print(a == 'not a point')

True False
{Point(1, 2)}
False

By default, == on your objects means is — identity, not equality — so two separately built points are unequal. Defining __eq__ fixes that. But defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None, making instances unhashable and unusable in a set or as a dict key, so you must define __hash__ too. The rule the two must obey together: equal objects must have equal hashes, which is why both are built from the same tuple. Returning NotImplemented (not False, and not the exception NotImplementedError) for a type you do not recognise lets Python try the other operand's __eq__ before falling back to False.

Then the protocols that make your object work with syntax:

class Playlist:
    def __init__(self, tracks):
        self.tracks = list(tracks)

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.tracks)

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        return self.tracks[index]

    def __contains__(self, track):
        return track in self.tracks

    def __iter__(self):
        return iter(self.tracks)

pl = Playlist(['Aja', 'Peg', 'Deacon Blues'])
print(len(pl))
print(pl[0], pl[-1])
print(pl[:2])
print('Peg' in pl)
print([t.upper() for t in pl])

3
Aja Deacon Blues
['Aja', 'Peg']
True
['AJA', 'PEG', 'DEACON BLUES']

Four small methods bought len(), indexing, slicing, in, and every form of iteration including comprehensions. This is what people mean by writing Pythonic classes: implement the protocol and the language's existing vocabulary applies to your type for free.

Arithmetic works the same way. a + b tries type(a).__add__(a, b):

class Money:
    def __init__(self, cents):
        self.cents = cents

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'{self.cents // 100}.{self.cents % 100:02d}'

    def __add__(self, other):
        return Money(self.cents + other.cents)

    def __mul__(self, n):
        return Money(self.cents * n)

    def __lt__(self, other):
        return self.cents < other.cents

print(Money(1250) + Money(399))
print(Money(1250) * 3)
print(sorted([Money(500), Money(120), Money(9999)]))

16.49
37.50
[1.20, 5.00, 99.99]

__lt__ alone was enough for sorted, because sorting only ever asks "is this less than that". The most useful dunders, in rough order of how often you will write them:

Method Triggered by Notes
__repr__ repr(x), the REPL, containers write this one always
__str__ str(x), print(x), f-strings falls back to __repr__
__eq__ x == y pair it with __hash__
__hash__ set, dict keys equal objects, equal hashes
__len__ len(x), truthiness zero length means falsey
__getitem__ x[k], slicing
__iter__ for, comprehensions, list(x) see §8
__contains__ in falls back to iteration
__lt__ and friends <, sorted, min, max functools.total_ordering fills in the rest
__add__, __mul__ … +, * one per operator
__enter__, __exit__ with see §9.11
__call__ x() makes the instance callable

One consequence worth knowing: __len__ also decides truthiness. An object with __len__ returning 0 is falsey in an if, which is usually what you want and is occasionally a surprise.

11.9 Multiple Inheritance and the MRO

A class may list more than one base:

class Serializable:
    def to_dict(self):
        return dict(self.__dict__)

class Comparable:
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return type(self) is type(other) and self.__dict__ == other.__dict__

class User(Serializable, Comparable):
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

u = User('ada')
print(u.to_dict())
print(u == User('ada'), u == User('bob'))

{'name': 'ada'}
True False

User gained methods from both bases. Used this way — small, single-purpose classes contributing behaviour, usually called mixins — multiple inheritance is genuinely useful. Used to model "a Dog is an Animal and also a Pet and also a Mammal", it usually creates more problems than it solves.

The problem it creates is which method wins. Python answers with the method resolution order (MRO): a single, fixed, linear order in which classes are searched, computed by an algorithm called C3 linearisation and readable on any class:

class A:
    def who(self): return 'A'
class B(A):
    def who(self): return 'B'
class C(A):
    def who(self): return 'C'
class D(B, C):
    pass

print([cls.__name__ for cls in D.__mro__])
print(D().who())

['D', 'B', 'C', 'A', 'object']
B

This shape — one base, two middles, one bottom — is the diamond, and the MRO resolves it: D, then B, then C, then A. D defines no who, so the search moves to B and stops there. B is checked before C because it was listed first, and A comes after both of them, never before, because a base class must not shadow something that derives from it.

You do not need to memorise C3. You need two facts. First, the order is left-to-right and depth-respecting, and __mro__ will tell you what it actually is. Second — and this is the practical one — super() follows the MRO, not the base class. That is a genuinely surprising and genuinely useful fact:

class A:
    def hello(self): return 'A'
class B(A):
    def hello(self): return 'B -> ' + super().hello()
class C(A):
    def hello(self): return 'C -> ' + super().hello()
class D(B, C):
    def hello(self): return 'D -> ' + super().hello()

print(D().hello())

D -> B -> C -> A

Read super() inside B and it looks like it must mean "call A.hello" — A is B's only base. It does not. In this object it means "call the next class after B in this instance's MRO", which is C. That is why super() is not a synonym for "the base class", and it is why the explicit A.hello(self) spelling would break this: it would skip C entirely and print D -> B -> A.

The practical rule for cooperative multiple inheritance: every class in the hierarchy uses super(), and __init__ methods accept and forward **kwargs so a class further along the MRO still receives what it needs.

11.10 Name Mangling and "Private" Attributes

Python has no private keyword and no enforced access control. It has two conventions and one mechanism.

A single leading underscore is the convention: self._balance means "this is internal, do not touch it from outside". Nothing prevents you. It is a note to other programmers, and the whole ecosystem — linters, documentation tools, from module import * — respects it.

A double leading underscore invokes the mechanism, called name mangling: inside a class body, __name is rewritten to _ClassName__name.

class Account:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.__balance = balance          # becomes self._Account__balance

    def peek(self):
        return self.__balance

a = Account(100)
print(a.peek())
try:
    print(a.__balance)
except AttributeError as e:
    print(e)
print(a._Account__balance)                # not private, just renamed
print(list(a.__dict__))

100
'Account' object has no attribute '__balance'
100
['_Account__balance']

Reading a.__balance from outside the class fails, because outside a class body no mangling happens and there really is no attribute of that name — the one that exists is _Account__balance, and printing it works fine. Mangling is not a security boundary; it is a collision-avoidance mechanism. Its actual purpose is to let a base class have an attribute that a subclass cannot accidentally clobber:

class Base:
    def __init__(self):
        self.__id = 'base'                # -> _Base__id
    def base_id(self):
        return self.__id

class Child(Base):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.__id = 'child'               # -> _Child__id, a *different* attribute
    def child_id(self):
        return self.__id

c = Child()
print(c.base_id(), c.child_id())
print(sorted(c.__dict__))

base child
['_Base__id', '_Child__id']

Had both been self._id, the child's assignment would have silently destroyed the base's state and base_id() would return 'child'. That is the bug mangling exists to prevent — and it is rare. Use a single underscore by default; reach for the double only in a class designed for subclassing where a name collision would be a real hazard.

11.11 property: a Method That Looks Like an Attribute

The trap in Account.balance from §11.1 was that nothing stops acct.balance = -900. The naive fix is to rename it _balance and add get_balance() and set_balance() methods — which works, and which makes every reader write acct.get_balance() where acct.balance would have read better.

property gives you the gate without the ceremony:

class Account:
    def __init__(self, balance=0):
        self._balance = balance

    @property
    def balance(self):
        return self._balance

    @balance.setter
    def balance(self, value):
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError('balance cannot be negative')
        self._balance = value

a = Account(100)
print(a.balance)               # calls the getter — no parentheses
a.balance = 250                # calls the setter
print(a.balance)
try:
    a.balance = -1
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)

100
250
balance cannot be negative

balance is a normal-looking attribute whose read and write run your code. Note the shape: the @property-decorated method defines the getter and gives the name; @balance.setter — the property's own decorator, not @property again — defines the setter. Omit the setter and the attribute becomes read-only, which is often exactly what you want:

class Circle:
    def __init__(self, radius):
        self.radius = radius

    @property
    def area(self):
        return 3.141592653589793 * self.radius ** 2

c = Circle(2)
print(round(c.area, 4))
c.radius = 3
print(round(c.area, 4))        # recomputed, never stale
try:
    c.area = 99
except AttributeError as e:
    print(e)

12.5664
28.2743
property 'area' of 'Circle' object has no setter

That is the other main use: a computed attribute. area is derived from radius, so storing it would risk the two disagreeing; a property recomputes on every read and cannot go stale.

The judgement call: do not start with properties. A plain public attribute is fine, and Python's great advantage over languages that need getters everywhere is that you can turn self.balance into a property later without changing a single line of calling code. Add the property when you actually have a rule to enforce or a value to compute.

11.12 dataclass: the Boilerplate, Written for You

A large fraction of real classes are records: some fields, an __init__ that assigns them, a __repr__, and equality by value. Written out, that is thirty lines in which the field names appear four times each. dataclasses in the standard library generates it:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float

p, q = Point(1, 2), Point(1, 2)
print(p)
print(p == q)
print(p.x)

Point(x=1, y=2)
True
1

Three lines gave a working __init__, a __repr__ that names its fields, and value equality. The annotations (§4.12) are how the decorator learns the field names, and they are required — a bare x with no annotation is not a field.

Defaults, computed fields and mutable fields:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Item:
    name: str
    price: float = 0.0
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    @property
    def price_with_tax(self):
        return round(self.price * 1.2, 2)

a = Item('book', 10.0)
b = Item('pen')
a.tags.append('paper')
print(a)
print(b)
print(a.price_with_tax)
print(Item('pen').tags is Item('nib').tags)     # a fresh list each time

Item(name='book', price=10.0, tags=['paper'])
Item(name='pen', price=0.0, tags=[])
12.0
False

A dataclass is a normal class: methods, properties and anything else you write in the body are kept as-is, and only the generated methods are added. Note that b got its own empty tags list rather than sharing a's.

field(default_factory=list) is the dataclass answer to the mutable-default trap: the factory is called per instance. Writing tags: list[str] = [] is rejected outright rather than silently sharing — one of the few places Python catches this class of mistake for you:

from dataclasses import dataclass

try:
    @dataclass
    class Bad:
        tags: list = []
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)

mutable default <class 'list'> for field tags is not allowed: use default_factory

Two options earn their keep immediately. frozen=True makes instances immutable and hashable, which is what you want for a value that should behave like a tuple:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Coord:
    lat: float
    lon: float

c = Coord(51.5, -0.1)
print({c, Coord(51.5, -0.1)})          # hashable: one entry
try:
    c.lat = 0
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e)

{Coord(lat=51.5, lon=-0.1)}
FrozenInstanceError cannot assign to field 'lat'

And order=True generates __lt__ and friends, so instances sort by their fields in declaration order:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(order=True)
class Version:
    major: int
    minor: int
    patch: int

vs = [Version(1, 2, 3), Version(1, 0, 0), Version(1, 2, 10)]
print(sorted(vs))
print(max(vs))

[Version(major=1, minor=0, patch=0), Version(major=1, minor=2, patch=3), Version(major=1, minor=2, patch=10)]
Version(major=1, minor=2, patch=10)

Reach for a dataclass by default when writing a class that is mostly fields. Write the class by hand when the __init__ does real work, when the object is defined by its behaviour rather than its data, or when you need an inheritance hierarchy with awkward defaults.

11.13 Composition, and When Not to Inherit

Inheritance is the most over-used feature in object-oriented programming, and the correction is a single question: is this an "is-a" or a "has-a"?

class Engine:
    def __init__(self, horsepower):
        self.horsepower = horsepower

    def start(self):
        return 'vroom'

class Car:
    def __init__(self, model, horsepower):
        self.model = model
        self.engine = Engine(horsepower)      # a car HAS an engine

    def start(self):
        return f'{self.model}: {self.engine.start()}'

print(Car('Saab 900', 145).start())

Saab 900: vroom

A car is not a kind of engine, so class Car(Engine) would be wrong — and it would leak, giving every Car a horsepower attribute at the top level and making isinstance(car, Engine) true. Composition — holding another object as an attribute — is the default, and inheritance is the special case where the derived thing genuinely is the base thing and can be used anywhere the base thing can.

The second question is whether you need a class at all. Playlist in §11.8 earned its keep. But this does not:

class Calculator:
    def add(self, a, b):
        return a + b

    def multiply(self, a, b):
        return a * b

calc = Calculator()
print(calc.add(2, 3), calc.multiply(2, 3))

5 6

There is no state. Calculator() exists only so that .add has something to hang off. Two module-level functions would be shorter, faster, easier to test and easier to import. In Python — unlike Java — a module is already a perfectly good namespace, so "grouping related functions" is not a reason to write a class.

Exercises

Exercise 11.1 — Two counters, one count. Explain the output, then fix the class so each counter is independent.

class Counter:
    count = 0

    def increment(self):
        self.count += 1

a, b = Counter(), Counter()
a.increment()
a.increment()
b.increment()
print(a.count, b.count, Counter.count)
Solution

The output is 2 1 0, and understanding why it is that rather than 3 3 3 or 2 1 3 is the whole exercise.

class Counter:
    count = 0

    def increment(self):
        self.count += 1

a, b = Counter(), Counter()
a.increment()
a.increment()
b.increment()
print(a.count, b.count, Counter.count)

2 1 0

self.count += 1 is self.count = self.count + 1. The right-hand side is a read, which finds nothing on the instance and falls back to the class variable 0. The left-hand side is an assignment, which — as §11.4 showed — always writes to the instance. So the first a.increment() reads the class's 0 and creates an instance attribute a.count = 1; every later call reads and writes the instance's own copy. The class variable is never touched.

This looks like it works: two counters really do count independently. It breaks the moment the value is mutable rather than rebound, because then there is no assignment to redirect it — which is the tricks = [] bug from §11.4. Relying on the difference is relying on a distinction most readers will not make.

The fix is to give each instance its own attribute explicitly:

class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0

    def increment(self):
        self.count += 1

a, b = Counter(), Counter()
a.increment(); a.increment(); b.increment()
print(a.count, b.count)

2 1

If you genuinely want a shared, class-wide total, be explicit about which one you are touching — and use a class method so there is no self to confuse it with:

class Counter:
    total = 0

    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0

    def increment(self):
        self.count += 1
        Counter.total += 1        # explicitly the class variable

a, b = Counter(), Counter()
a.increment(); a.increment(); b.increment()
print(a.count, b.count, Counter.total)

2 1 3

Exercise 11.2 — A Vector you can use. Write a Vector class holding x and y such that all of the following work: printing shows Vector(3, 4), two vectors with the same components are equal and can go in a set, + and - combine them, * scales by a number, abs() gives the length, and bool() is false for the zero vector.

Solution

Each requirement maps to exactly one dunder, which is the point of the exercise — "make it printable" is __repr__, "make it addable" is __add__, and there is no cleverness in between.

import math

class Vector:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Vector({self.x}, {self.y})'

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Vector):
            return NotImplemented
        return (self.x, self.y) == (other.x, other.y)

    def __hash__(self):
        return hash((self.x, self.y))

    def __add__(self, other):
        return Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y)

    def __sub__(self, other):
        return Vector(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y)

    def __mul__(self, k):
        return Vector(self.x * k, self.y * k)

    def __abs__(self):
        return math.hypot(self.x, self.y)

    def __bool__(self):
        return bool(self.x or self.y)

v = Vector(3, 4)
print(v)
print(v + Vector(1, 1), v - Vector(1, 1), v * 2)
print(abs(v))
print(bool(v), bool(Vector(0, 0)))
print(Vector(1, 2) == Vector(1, 2), len({Vector(1, 2), Vector(1, 2)}))

Vector(3, 4)
Vector(4, 5) Vector(2, 3) Vector(6, 8)
5.0
True False
True 1

Three things worth noticing.

Every operator returns a new Vector rather than mutating self. That is what makes v + w behave the way 1 + 2 does, and it is why v is unchanged after all those lines.

2 * v does not work yet. Python tries int.__mul__(2, v), which returns NotImplemented, and then tries the reflected method Vector.__rmul__. Add __rmul__ = __mul__ to the class body and both orders work.

__bool__ was needed because without it Python would fall back to __len__, and with neither defined every object is truthy — including the zero vector. Defining __bool__ is the only way to make an object falsey when it has no meaningful length.

Exercise 11.3 — Fix the hierarchy. This code runs, but two of the three classes have a real design fault. Identify both and rewrite.

class Config:
    settings = {}

    def set(self, key, value):
        self.settings[key] = value

class Timestamped(Config):
    def __init__(self, created_at):
        self.created_at = created_at

class Document(Timestamped):
    def __init__(self, title, created_at):
        self.title = title
Solution

Fault one: Config.settings is a mutable class variable (§11.4). Every object that inherits from Config — anywhere in the program — shares one dictionary, so a setting written by one document appears in all of them.

Fault two: Document.__init__ never calls super().__init__() (§11.7), so created_at is never set. The object constructs perfectly happily and blows up later, somewhere else, with an AttributeError.

Here is the fault demonstrated before it is fixed, because seeing it fail is more convincing than being told:

class Config:
    settings = {}
    def set(self, key, value):
        self.settings[key] = value

class Timestamped(Config):
    def __init__(self, created_at):
        self.created_at = created_at

class Document(Timestamped):
    def __init__(self, title, created_at):
        self.title = title

a = Document('A', '2026-01-01')
b = Document('B', '2026-06-01')
a.set('theme', 'dark')
print(b.settings)                       # leaked from a
try:
    print(a.created_at)
except AttributeError as e:
    print(e)

{'theme': 'dark'}
'Document' object has no attribute 'created_at'

The rewrite fixes both, and takes the opportunity to ask the §11.13 question: is a document a kind of config? It is not. Config is a thing a document has, so the inheritance chain becomes composition:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Config:
    settings: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def set(self, key, value):
        self.settings[key] = value

@dataclass
class Document:
    title: str
    created_at: str
    config: Config = field(default_factory=Config)

a = Document('A', '2026-01-01')
b = Document('B', '2026-06-01')
a.config.set('theme', 'dark')
print(a.config.settings, b.config.settings)
print(a.created_at)
print(a)

{'theme': 'dark'} {}
2026-01-01
Document(title='A', created_at='2026-01-01', config=Config(settings={'theme': 'dark'}))

default_factory (§11.12) removes the shared-mutable fault by construction, the dataclass-generated __init__ removes the forgotten-super() fault by there being no hand-written __init__ to forget it in, and composition removes an inheritance relationship that was never true. Three faults, and the fix for each was to write less code.

SECTION 12

Modules, Packages and Environments

A program that fits in one file stops being one soon enough. Splitting it up is not just tidiness — it is what makes a codebase navigable, testable and reusable. Python's answer is the module, the package, and an import system with a small number of rules that explain every "why can't it find my file" error you will ever hit. This section also covers the other half of the same problem: which Python is running, and which packages it can see.

12.1 A Module Is a File

Any .py file is a module, and importing it runs it once and gives you a namespace holding everything it defined.

$ cat geometry.py
"""Simple plane geometry."""
PI = 3.141592653589793

def circle_area(radius):
    return PI * radius ** 2

def rectangle_area(width, height):
    return width * height

print('geometry module is being executed')

$ python3
>>> import geometry
geometry module is being executed
>>> geometry.circle_area(2)
12.566370614359172
>>> geometry.PI
3.141592653589793
>>> import geometry          # imported again: the body does NOT run twice
>>> geometry.__name__, geometry.__file__.endswith('geometry.py')
('geometry', True)

Two facts there matter more than they look. Importing executes the module's top level, which is why the print fired — so anything at the top level of a module happens as a side effect of importing it. And it happens only once per interpreter: subsequent imports find the module in sys.modules and hand back the same object.

import sys

print('json' in sys.modules)
import json
print('json' in sys.modules)
print(sys.modules['json'] is json)

False
True
True

That caching is what makes circular and repeated imports affordable, and it is also why editing a module does not affect an already-running interpreter.

12.2 The Four Forms of the Import Statement

import math                              # the module, reached by name
from math import sqrt, pi                # specific names, straight into your namespace
from math import sqrt as square_root     # renamed
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET       # a nested module, aliased

print(math.sqrt(16), sqrt(16), square_root(16))
print(round(pi, 4))
print(ET.__name__)

4.0 4.0 4.0
3.1416
xml.etree.ElementTree

Which form of the import statement to use is a real judgement, not a style preference:

import module — the default. Keeps the origin visible at the call site: math.sqrt says where sqrt came from, and cannot collide with a sqrt of your own.
from module import name — for a handful of names used constantly, where the prefix would be noise: from pathlib import Path, from dataclasses import dataclass.
import module as alias — for long names and community conventions: import numpy as np, import pandas as pd.
from module import * — avoid. It imports every public name at once, so you cannot tell where anything came from and a new release of the module can silently shadow your own names.

The star-import problem is worth seeing rather than being warned about:

def open(path):
    return f'my own open: {path}'

print(open('a.txt'))
from os import *                 # brings in os.open, which is completely different
print(open.__module__)

my own open: a.txt
posix

The function was replaced. Nothing warned, and the next call to open gets a low-level file-descriptor function with a different signature. In a script of a hundred lines this is a puzzling afternoon.

dir() is how you find out what a module actually contains, which is useful at the REPL and in debugging:

import math

names = [n for n in dir(math) if not n.startswith('_')]
print(len(names), 'public names')
print(names[:8])
print([n for n in names if 'sqrt' in n])

62 public names
['acos', 'acosh', 'asin', 'asinh', 'atan', 'atan2', 'atanh', 'cbrt']
['isqrt', 'sqrt']

dir() with no argument lists the names in the current scope, and dir(obj) lists an object's attributes — including methods, which makes it the fastest way to ask "what can I do with this thing".

12.3 The Module Search Path

When you write import geometry, Python looks for it in sys.path, in order, and takes the first match.

$ python3 -c "import sys
for e in sys.path[:6]: print(repr(e))"
''
'/usr/lib/python314.zip'
'/usr/lib/python3.14'
'/usr/lib/python3.14/lib-dynload'
'/usr/local/lib/python3.14/dist-packages'
'/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages'

The list is assembled from three sources: the directory of the script being run (or '', meaning the current directory, when you are at the REPL), then anything in the PYTHONPATH environment variable, then the interpreter's own standard library and site-packages directories.

"First match wins" is the whole explanation for the single most confusing beginner error in Python:

$ ls
random.py    main.py

$ cat random.py
print('this is my file, not the standard library')

$ cat main.py
import random
print(random.randint(1, 6))

$ python3 main.py
this is my file, not the standard library
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(random.randint(1, 6))
          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: module 'random' has no attribute 'randint'

The script's own directory comes first on sys.path, so random.py shadows the standard library module of the same name. The error is bewildering — "random has no randint" — until you know the rule. Never name a file after a standard-library module: random.py, json.py, string.py, email.py, types.py and test.py are all traps. If you have already done it, deleting the stray .pyc in __pycache__ may also be necessary.

That __pycache__ directory is the other thing you will notice. Python compiles each module to bytecode on first import and caches it there, keyed by interpreter version:

$ ls __pycache__/
geometry.cpython-314.pyc

It is a cache and nothing more — safe to delete, automatically regenerated, invalidated when the source's timestamp and size change. It belongs in .gitignore, never in version control.

12.4 __name__ and if __name__ == '__main__'

Every module has a __name__. When it is imported, __name__ is the module's name. When it is run directly as a script, __name__ is the string '__main__'.

$ cat greet.py
def greet(name):
    return f'Hello, {name}!'

print(f'__name__ is {__name__!r}')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    print(greet('world'))

$ python3 greet.py
__name__ is '__main__'
Hello, world!

$ python3 -c "import greet"
__name__ is 'greet'

Run directly, the guarded block executed. Imported, it did not.

This is the mechanism that lets one file be both a library and a command. Without the guard, importing greet to use its function would also run the demonstration — and in a real module, that might mean starting a server, connecting to a database, or reading sys.argv that belongs to a different program.

The pattern to write, with the process concerns kept out of the logic:

$ cat report.py
import sys

def summarise(rows):
    """Pure function: no I/O, no sys.argv, trivially testable."""
    return {'rows': len(rows), 'total': sum(r['amount'] for r in rows)}

def main(argv=None):
    argv = sys.argv[1:] if argv is None else argv
    if not argv:
        print('usage: report.py FILE', file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    print(summarise([{'amount': 10}, {'amount': 32}]))
    return 0

if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main())

summarise can be imported and tested without a file or a command line; main returns a status rather than calling sys.exit itself, so a test can check it; and only the last two lines connect the module to a process.

12.5 Packages: a Directory of Modules

A package is a directory that Python treats as a module. Put related modules inside it and the directory name becomes a namespace.

shop/
├── __init__.py
├── models.py
├── pricing.py
└── storage/
    ├── __init__.py
    └── sqlite.py

$ cat shop/__init__.py
"""The shop package."""
__version__ = '1.0.0'

$ cat shop/pricing.py
TAX_RATE = 0.2

def with_tax(amount):
    return round(amount * (1 + TAX_RATE), 2)

$ python3
>>> import shop.pricing
>>> shop.pricing.with_tax(100)
120.0
>>> from shop.pricing import with_tax
>>> with_tax(50)
60.0
>>> import shop
>>> shop.__version__
'1.0.0'

__init__.py marks the directory as a package and runs when the package is first imported. It is very often empty, and that is fine — its presence is the point. Two things it is legitimately used for: setting package-level metadata such as __version__, and re-exporting a convenient public surface so users write from shop import with_tax instead of from shop.pricing import with_tax.

$ cat shop/__init__.py
"""The shop package."""
__version__ = '1.0.0'

from shop.pricing import with_tax
from shop.models import Product

__all__ = ['with_tax', 'Product', '__version__']

__all__ declares the public names — it controls what from shop import * brings in, and it documents intent for readers and tools. Keep __init__.py cheap: anything expensive there is paid by everyone who imports any part of the package.

Since Python 3.3 a directory without __init__.py can still be imported, as a namespace package. That exists to let one package be split across several directories, and for ordinary work it mostly causes confusion — a typo in a directory name produces a silently empty package rather than an error. Include __init__.py.

12.6 Absolute and Relative Imports

Inside a package, a module can refer to its siblings two ways.

$ cat shop/models.py
from shop.pricing import with_tax          # absolute: from the top of the package

class Product:
    def __init__(self, name, net):
        self.name, self.net = name, net

    @property
    def gross(self):
        return with_tax(self.net)

$ cat shop/storage/sqlite.py
from ..pricing import with_tax             # relative: one level up, then pricing
from .  import __name__ as here            # relative: this package

def save(product):
    return f'saving {product.name} at {with_tax(product.net)}'

A relative import uses leading dots: one dot means "this package", two means "the parent package", three means the grandparent. It is shorter, and it survives the package being renamed or vendored into another project.

An absolute import names the full path from the top. It is unambiguous, it reads the same wherever it appears, and it is what PEP 8 recommends as the default.

The rule that avoids trouble: use absolute imports across packages and prefer them within a package too; use relative imports only for genuinely sibling modules in the same package, and never go up more than one level. A from ...core.utils import x is a sign the package structure needs rethinking.

There is one hard constraint. A relative import only works inside a package, so a module using one cannot be run directly as a script:

$ python3 shop/storage/sqlite.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "shop/storage/sqlite.py", line 1, in <module>
    from ..pricing import with_tax
ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package

Run as a script, sqlite.py has __name__ == '__main__' and no package context, so ".." refers to nothing. The fix is to run it as a module, which gives Python the package context:

$ python3 -m shop.storage.sqlite

python3 -m package.module is worth knowing generally: it is how you run python3 -m pytest, python3 -m http.server, python3 -m venv and python3 -m json.tool.

12.7 Circular Imports

Two modules that import each other will usually work, and will sometimes fail in a way that looks like nonsense:

$ cat a.py
import b
def hello(): return 'hello from a'
print('a loaded; b.value is', b.value)

$ cat b.py
import a
value = 42
print('b loaded; a.hello is', a.hello())

$ python3 -c "import a"
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File "b.py", line 3, in <module>
    print('b loaded; a.hello is', a.hello())
                                  ^^^^^^^
AttributeError: partially initialized module 'a' has no attribute 'hello'
  (most likely due to a circular import)

The sequence: importing a starts executing a.py; line 1 imports b; b.py starts executing; its line 1 imports a, finds a partially initialised a already in sys.modules, and gets it back immediately — but a.hello has not been defined yet, because a.py is still on its first line.

Python's error message names the cause, which is a mercy. Three fixes, in order of preference:

Restructure. A circular import nearly always means the two modules share something that belongs in a third. Move value and hello into common.py and have both import that.

Import inside the function. Deferring the import until call time means the module is fully loaded by then:

$ cat b.py
value = 42

def describe():
    import a                     # deferred: a is fully loaded by the time this runs
    return a.hello()

Import the module, not the name. import a then a.hello() works where from a import hello fails, because the attribute is looked up at call time rather than at import time.

12.8 Virtual Environments

Every Python installation has one site-packages directory. Install everything into it and two projects that need different versions of the same library cannot both work — and, worse, a project that works on your machine depends on the accumulated history of everything you have ever installed.

A virtual environment is a private directory holding its own interpreter link and its own site-packages. One per project.

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

$ python3 -m venv .venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ which python3
/home/ada/project/.venv/bin/python3
(.venv) $ python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"
/home/ada/project/.venv
(.venv) $ deactivate
$ which python3
/usr/bin/python3

On Windows the activation line is .venv\Scripts\activate instead.

What activate actually does is small and worth knowing: it puts .venv/bin at the front of your PATH and sets a VIRTUAL_ENV variable. That is all. So the environment is not magic and it is not global state — it applies to the shell you ran it in, and only until you close that shell.

$ ls .venv/
bin  include  lib  lib64  pyvenv.cfg
$ ls .venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/ | head -3
pip
pip-25.2.dist-info

Three rules:

One environment per project, named .venv in the project directory. That convention is what lets editors and tools find it automatically.

Never commit .venv to version control. It contains platform-specific binaries and is entirely reproducible from a requirements file. Put .venv/ in .gitignore.

If you are not sure which Python you are running, ask. which python3 and python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)" answer it in one line each, and a startling proportion of "the package is installed but Python cannot find it" problems are answered right there.

12.9 pip and Requirements

pip installs packages from PyPI, the Python Package Index, into the environment that is currently active.

python3 -m pip install requests
python3 -m pip install 'requests>=2.31,<3'
python3 -m pip list
python3 -m pip show requests
python3 -m pip uninstall requests

Write python3 -m pip, not bare pip. The -m form guarantees you are installing into the interpreter you just named. A bare pip is whatever the shell's PATH finds first, which — outside an activated environment, or with several Pythons installed — is regularly not the one you think.

Recording dependencies so that someone else can reproduce your environment:

$ python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
$ cat requirements.txt
certifi==2026.6.15
charset-normalizer==3.4.2
idna==3.10
requests==2.32.4
urllib3==2.5.0

$ python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt

pip freeze writes every installed package with an exact version — including the ones installed as dependencies of dependencies, which is why the file above has five entries for one pip install requests. That exactness is the point: it is what makes the environment reproducible on another machine.

The distinction worth understanding is direct dependencies versus pinned versions. requirements.txt from freeze is a snapshot: precise, reproducible, and silent about which of those five you actually asked for. Modern projects declare their direct dependencies with loose constraints in pyproject.toml and generate an exact lockfile from it:

$ cat pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "shop"
version = "1.0.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "requests>=2.31",
]

For a first project, requirements.txt is entirely adequate and one command to produce. The important habits are that the file exists, that it is committed, and that a new contributor can go from a fresh clone to a working environment in three commands:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt

A last note on tooling: uv is a much faster drop-in replacement for pip and venv that has become common, and pipx installs command-line applications into their own isolated environments so they do not pollute a project's. Both are worth knowing about; neither changes anything in this section, because they implement the same model.

12.10 Laying Out a Project

Putting the pieces together, this is a shape that works from the first day and keeps working:

shop/
├── .gitignore
├── README.md
├── requirements.txt
├── src/
│   └── shop/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── models.py
│       ├── pricing.py
│       └── cli.py
└── tests/
    ├── test_models.py
    └── test_pricing.py

Four decisions are encoded there.

The package lives under src/. This is not decoration: without it, running the tests from the project root puts the project root on sys.path, so import shop finds the source directory rather than the installed package — and a test suite that accidentally tests the source tree rather than what you ship will not notice a file you forgot to include. With src/, the only way to import shop is to have installed it.

Tests live outside the package, in a directory of their own, so they are not shipped to users and are not importable as part of the library.

.gitignore covers the generated things: __pycache__/, *.pyc, .venv/, and whatever your tools produce.

README.md says what it is and how to run it. Three commands and a sentence beats none.

To make the package importable while you work on it, install it in editable mode, which puts a link to your source directory into the environment rather than a copy:

python3 -m pip install -e .

Now import shop works from anywhere in the environment, and your edits take effect without reinstalling. This one command resolves most of the "how do my tests import my code" confusion that otherwise leads people to sys.path.append(...) — which works, and which you should not do.

Exercises
